A course text on the RTL-to-GDSII flow: logic synthesis, floorplanning, placement, clock-tree synthesis, routing, static timing analysis, physical verification and tapeout, with worked examples, exercises and a hands-on OpenLANE and Sky130 laboratory.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Clock-Tree Synthesis
docs.text:
A data net connects a handful of pins. The clock net connects every flip-flop in the block, often tens of thousands of them, and every one must be told "now" at very nearly the same instant. No single gate can drive that much wire: the edge would crawl, and the flip-flops nearest the source would be clocked long before the farthest ones. Until now the clock has been treated as ideal, infinitely strong and arriving everywhere at once. Clock-tree synthesis (CTS) replaces that fiction with a real, buffered network.

Think of a starting pistol for ten thousand runners spread across a city. You cannot simply shout; you need relay stations so that everyone hears "go" at the same moment. This chapter defines the two numbers that describe how well the relays do their job, latency and skew; shows how skew moves the setup and hold slack; compares the three ways of building the tree; and explains what changes once the clock is real, above all that hold is repaired for the first time.

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you can:

  1. Explain why the clock net is special and what CTS builds.
  2. Define latency and skew and compute skew from two latencies.
  3. Show how positive and negative skew move setup and hold slack.
  4. Compare buffer trees, H-trees and meshes, and describe useful skew and clock gating.
  5. Describe the post-CTS flow: propagated clock, setup re-check and hold repair.

docs.title: 5.1 Why the clock is special
docs.text:
During synthesis and placement the clock is ideal: it is assumed to reach every flip-flop at once with zero delay. CTS makes it real by building a balanced tree of clock buffers or inverters from the clock source out to every flip-flop, so that arrival times stay tightly matched despite real wire delay. Afterwards the clock is propagated: timing analysis uses the actual delay to every flip-flop, and the timing is checked again against that reality.

The input to the stage is a floorplanned, placed and legalised design, optimised for setup against the ideal clock. Its output is the same design with a real clock tree and propagated (post-CTS) timing, ready for routing.

docs.title: 5.2 Two numbers: latency and skew
docs.text:
Latency, also called insertion delay, is the delay from the clock source (a port or a PLL output) to the clock pin of a given flip-flop. It has two parts: source latency (from the source to the block's clock root) and network latency (from the root to the flip-flop, built by CTS). Low latency is nice, but equal latency is what matters.

Skew is the difference in clock arrival time between two flip-flops:

\[\text{skew} = \text{latency}_{\text{capture}} - \text{latency}_{\text{launch}}\]

CTS aims for a global skew near zero so that the whole design sees the edge together. Skew is what actually eats into timing margins.

Example 5.1: Latency and skew

The delay from the clock source to the clock pin of FF_A is 412 ps and to FF_B is 468 ps. For a path from FF_A (launch) to FF_B (capture),

\[\text{skew} = 468 - 412 = +56 \text{ ps}.\]

Skew is positive: the capture clock arrives later than the launch clock (Figure 5.1).

Figure 5.1 Latency and skew. Two arrows from the clock source, 412 ps to FF_A and 468 ps to FF_B, with the 56 ps difference marked as skew.

docs.title: 5.3 How skew moves the slack
docs.text:
Skew changes the timing budget directly. With a launch-clock arrival \(t_{launch}\) and a capture-clock arrival \(t_{capture}\), the skew is \(t_{skew} = t_{capture} - t_{launch}\), and the slack formulas of Chapter 2 become

\[\text{setup slack} = (T + t_{skew} - t_{su}) - (t_{cq} + t_{logic,max})\] \[\text{hold slack} = (t_{cq} + t_{logic,min}) - (t_h + t_{skew})\]
  • Positive skew (the capture clock is later) gives the data extra time to arrive, so it helps setup; but the capture flip-flop keeps listening for longer after the edge, so it hurts hold.
  • Negative skew (the capture clock is earlier) does the reverse: it helps hold and hurts setup.

That is why CTS drives skew towards zero: neither check is starved, and both budgets stay balanced and predictable across thousands of endpoints. Deliberate skew is used only surgically (Section 5.5).

Example 5.2: One path, setup and hold, with skew

Take the path from FF_A to FF_B of Example 5.1, with \(T = 1000\) ps (1 GHz), \(t_{cq} = 90\) ps, slowest logic 700 ps, fastest logic 120 ps, \(t_{su} = 60\) ps and \(t_h = 40\) ps. The skew is \(+56\) ps.

Setup.

  1. Arrival \(= t_{cq} + t_{logic,max} = 90 + 700 = 790\) ps (measured from the launch edge).
  2. Required \(= T + t_{skew} - t_{su} = 1000 + 56 - 60 = 996\) ps.
  3. Slack \(= 996 - 790 = +206\) ps. Met; the positive skew added 56 ps of margin.

Hold.

  1. Arrival of the earliest new data \(= t_{cq} + t_{logic,min} = 90 + 120 = 210\) ps.
  2. Requirement \(= t_h + t_{skew} = 40 + 56 = 96\) ps.
  3. Slack \(= 210 - 96 = +114\) ps. Met.

If the skew grows to +180 ps: hold slack \(= 210 - (40 + 180) = -10\) ps, a hold violation. The skew that helped setup has eaten the hold margin. (Setup would still be \(1000 + 180 - 60 - 790 = +330\) ps.)

docs.title: 5.4 Three ways to build the tree
docs.text:
CTS balances arrival times by choosing a topology for the buffered network, and by sizing and placing its buffers so that every leaf path has matched delay. Figure 5.2 contrasts a single long wire with a balanced H-tree.

Figure 5.2 One wire versus a balanced tree. Left: one wire from the clock source to four flip-flops, with wires of different lengths. Right: an H-shaped tree with clock buffers at its joints so that every flip-flop is at the same wire distance from the root. Structure Idea Strengths Costs Buffer or inverter tree recursively cluster nearby flip-flops, drive each cluster with a buffer, drive those buffers from the next level up; the default in TritonCTS scales to millions of flip-flops; flexible; low area compared with a mesh; skew tuned per branch skew grows with depth; sensitive to on-chip variation along long branches H-tree a geometrically symmetric, fractal H shape so that every leaf is the same wire distance from the root excellent balance by construction; good for regular arrays and top-level distribution rigid; wastes wire when flip-flops are unevenly spread; hard on irregular floorplans Clock mesh or grid a dense metal grid driven from many points; flip-flops tap the nearest node very low skew and robust against variation; used in high-performance CPUs and GPUs large power and metal cost; complex to build and verify

Table 5.1 Three clock-distribution structures.

Two further techniques are applied on top of the balanced tree.

Useful skew. Instead of forcing zero skew everywhere, the tool can deliberately delay or advance a flip-flop's clock to lend time across a boundary: a tight path is given more setup room by delaying its capture clock, with the time borrowed from a neighbouring path that has margin to spare. It is applied path by path.

Clock gating. The clock network is often the single largest consumer of power, because it toggles every cycle across the whole chip. Clock-gating cells (integrated clock-gate, ICG, cells) switch the clock off to idle register banks. CTS must balance the tree through these gates so that the enable logic does not introduce skew.

docs.title: 5.5 After the tree: a real clock and hold repair
docs.text:
Once the tree exists, the clock becomes propagated, and two things happen.

Setup is re-verified. The clock buffers' own delays and the real skew shift every path's budget. Small setup regressions are cleaned up with further sizing and buffering, now against the true clock.

Hold is fixed for the first time. With an ideal clock hold looked fine everywhere. With the real clock, short paths between flip-flops whose clocks arrive at different times can now violate hold. The remedy is to slow the data path down: insert delay (hold) buffers on the short paths so that \(t_{cq} + t_{logic,min}\) grows past \(t_h + t_{skew}\).

# OpenROAD / TritonCTS: build the tree, then propagate and fix hold
clock_tree_synthesis -buf_list {sky130_fd_sc_hd__clkbuf_4 \
                                sky130_fd_sc_hd__clkbuf_8} \
                     -root_buf sky130_fd_sc_hd__clkbuf_16 \
                     -sink_clustering_enable

set_propagated_clock [all_clocks]           ;# from ideal to real clock
estimate_parasitics -placement
repair_timing -hold -hold_margin 0.05       ;# insert hold buffers on short paths
report_clock_skew                           ;# check the global skew achieved

In OpenLANE the stage is controlled by CTS_* variables in config.tcl:

set ::env(CTS_CLK_BUFFER_LIST)      "sky130_fd_sc_hd__clkbuf_4 sky130_fd_sc_hd__clkbuf_8"
set ::env(CTS_ROOT_BUFFER)          "sky130_fd_sc_hd__clkbuf_16"
set ::env(CTS_TARGET_SKEW)          "50"      ;# target skew, ps
set ::env(CTS_TOLERANCE)            "100"
set ::env(CTS_SINK_CLUSTERING_SIZE) "25"
set ::env(CLOCK_PORT)               "clk"
set ::env(CLOCK_PERIOD)             "10.0"    ;# ns

Reports for the stage land in runs/<tag>/reports/cts/.

Think about it

Why not fix hold earlier, during placement?

Answer

Hold depends on the real clock arrival times, which do not exist until the tree is built. A hold fix made against an ideal clock would be guesswork, and would waste buffers that must then be redone.

Before CTS (ideal clock) After CTS (propagated clock) Clock network does not exist buffers placed and connected (routed next) Skew assumed 0 real, small, non-zero (target near CTS_TARGET_SKEW) Latency 0 (or a modelled estimate) actual: hundreds of picoseconds Setup work done here: buffer, size, clone data paths re-checked and touched up against the real clock Hold work deferred: meaningless with an ideal clock done here: delay buffers on short paths Clock power not modelled significant, often the largest single item

Table 5.2 Before and after the clock tree.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Placement and early optimisation use an ideal clock. CTS replaces it with a buffered network (a buffer tree, an H-tree or a mesh) that delivers the edge to every flip-flop at nearly the same time.
  • Latency is the delay from the clock source to one flip-flop; skew is the difference between two flip-flops, capture minus launch.
  • Positive skew helps setup and hurts hold; negative skew does the reverse. CTS keeps skew near zero, with useful skew and clock gating applied deliberately.
  • After CTS the clock is propagated, setup is re-checked, and hold is repaired for the first time by inserting delay buffers on short paths.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 5.1: Skew of three paths

Clock latencies are FF1 310 ps, FF2 355 ps, FF3 290 ps, FF4 340 ps. The paths are FF1 to FF2, FF3 to FF4 and FF2 to FF3. Find the skew of each. Which path is most at risk for hold, and which for setup?

Answer

FF1 to FF2: \(355 - 310 = +45\) ps. FF3 to FF4: \(340 - 290 = +50\) ps. FF2 to FF3: \(290 - 355 = -65\) ps. Positive skew eats hold, so FF3 to FF4 (+50 ps) is most at risk for hold. Negative skew eats setup, so FF2 to FF3 (−65 ps) is most at risk for setup.

Exercise 5.2: Which check does it hurt?

Launch latency is 300 ps and capture latency is 250 ps. What is the skew, and which check does it hurt?

Answer

\(250 - 300 = -50\) ps, negative skew. The capture clock is early, so it hurts setup and helps hold.

Exercise 5.3: How much skew can hold take?

For the path of Example 5.2, find the largest skew for which hold slack is still non-negative, and the most negative skew for which setup slack is still non-negative.

Answer

Hold: \(210 - (40 + s) \ge 0\) gives \(s \le 170\) ps. Setup: \(1000 + s - 60 - 790 \ge 0\) gives \(s \ge -150\) ps. So this path tolerates skew from \(-150\) ps to \(+170\) ps. At \(+180\) ps (Example 5.2) it fails hold by 10 ps, as shown.

Exercise 5.4: Repairing the hold violation

In the +180 ps case of Example 5.2, how much delay must be inserted on the short path to repair hold, and does setup still pass?

Answer

Hold slack was \(-10\) ps, so at least 10 ps of extra minimum delay is needed (in practice a little more, as a hold margin). Even if the buffer's delay were added to the slowest route as well, setup slack would fall only from \(+330\) ps to about \(+320\) ps, so setup still passes comfortably.

Exercise 5.5: Why not a mesh everywhere?

A mesh gives the lowest skew. Why is a buffer tree the default?

Answer

A mesh costs a great deal of power and metal and is complex to build and verify. A buffer tree scales to millions of flip-flops at much lower area, and its skew can be tuned per branch; the small extra skew is acceptable for most designs. Meshes are kept for the highest-performance CPUs and GPUs.

docs.title: Chapter 3: Floorplanning and Power Planning
docs.text:
Synthesis hands the back end a gate-level netlist: a huge, position-less bag of standard cells and macros. Floorplanning is where that netlist first becomes a physical object. We decide how big the die is, what shape it has, where the memories and the input and output pins sit, and how power will reach every cell. These decisions are made before a single cell is placed, and every later stage, placement, clock-tree synthesis, routing and timing, can only optimise inside the box that the floorplan draws. A poor floorplan cannot be rescued by clever placement or routing; it has to be thrown away and redone. That is why this short chapter is worth more care per page than any other in the back end.

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you can:

  1. List what a floorplan fixes and explain why every later stage is bound by it.
  2. Tell the die from the core, and explain rows, sites and cell orientation.
  3. Choose a utilisation and compute core and die size from it.
  4. Describe the power grid (rings, straps, rails, vias) and why IR drop and electromigration make it matter.
  5. Place macros with halos, plan pins, and read the main OpenLANE floorplan variables.

docs.title: 3.1 What floorplanning decides
docs.text:
Floorplanning is the first physical step of the flow. Before anything is placed, it fixes:

  • Size: the total silicon area that you will pay the foundry for, and the usable region inside it.
  • Shape: the aspect ratio, height divided by width, of the core. It affects routing and how the block tiles into a larger chip.
  • Pins: where signals and power enter and leave the block.
  • Macros: where the large fixed blocks go: memories, clock generators, analogue parts. Placement must route around them.
  • Power: the distribution network, built before placement so that cells snap onto power.

Why it is the most consequential step

Placement, clock-tree synthesis, routing and timing all optimise within the box that floorplanning draws. A die that is too small, a macro that blocks a critical path or a weak power grid cannot be repaired later without ripping up the floorplan and starting again. Effort spent here pays back at every stage that follows. (Compare planning a building before the furniture arrives: move a stairwell later and everything else moves with it.)

docs.title: 3.2 Die and core, rows and sites
docs.text:
Two nested rectangles define the block's geometry (Figure 3.1).

Figure 3.1 Die, core, margin, macro, halo and pins. A die with a dashed core inside it, I/O pins on the die edge, a macro with a halo against the core edge, and standard-cell rows filling the rest of the core. Term Meaning Die area the whole piece of silicon, edge to edge, including any I/O ring or pad frame Core area the inner region where standard cells and macros are placed and routed Core margin the gap between the core boundary and the die edge, reserved for pins, the power ring and routing to pins; typically 10 to 30 µm per side Rows horizontal tracks, each one cell high, that tile the core; adjacent rows are flipped so that they share power and ground rails Sites the unit grid within a row; a cell's width is a whole number of sites, its height is one row; in the Sky130 unithd library a site is 0.46 µm × 2.72 µm Orientation each instance has an orientation (R0, MX, MY, R180 and so on); row flipping (MX) lets neighbouring rows abut VDD to VDD and VSS to VSS

Table 3.1 The vocabulary of floorplan geometry.

Every other row is flipped upside down, so that a rail is shared between two rows: VDD meets VDD and ground meets ground (Figure 3.2). Cells snap onto the site grid, and the placer is free to choose the orientation each row requires.

Figure 3.2 Rows, sites and row flipping. Two adjacent standard-cell rows sharing a VSS rail, with the site grid drawn, an upright cell in the first row and a flipped cell in the second.

Hard macros, such as compiled SRAM blocks, are placed first and usually pushed towards the edges or corners of the core so that they do not fragment the sea of standard-cell rows. Pins (in a block flow) or bonding pads (in a padded chip flow) are assigned to the die edges: data pins on the sides, and dedicated power and ground pins feeding the ring.

docs.title: 3.3 Utilisation: how full is the core?
docs.text:
Utilisation is the most important single number in a floorplan.

Definition: utilisation

Utilisation = total standard-cell area ÷ core area. At 0.70, cells cover 70 % of the core; the other 30 % is whitespace left for wiring, extra buffers, clock cells and legalisation.

Typical initial targets are 60 to 75 %. The trade-off is fundamental.

Utilisation Die size and cost Routability Verdict Low, about 50 % large, expensive, silicon wasted easy: plenty of room for wires wasteful 60 to 75 % reasonable congestion manageable the usual choice Above 85 % small, cheap congested, hard to route, timing suffers risky

Table 3.2 The utilisation trade-off.

A denser design looks cheaper, until a design that will not route, or that fails timing because there is no room to buffer a long net, costs weeks of extra iterations. Choose a target that leaves room for the clock buffers and repair buffers that later stages will add.

Example 3.1: Sizing a block

A block has 20 000 cells averaging 2 µm². Target utilisation 70 %, a square core, a margin of 20 µm.

  1. Total cell area \(= 20\,000 \times 2 = 40\,000\) µm².
  2. Core area \(= 40\,000 / 0.70 \approx 57\,143\) µm².
  3. A square core has side \(\sqrt{57\,143} \approx 239\) µm.
  4. The die adds the margin on both sides of each dimension: \(239 + 2 \times 20 \approx 279\) µm.
  5. Die area \(= 279 \times 279 \approx 77\,800\) µm².

At 80 % utilisation the core shrinks to \(40\,000 / 0.80 = 50\,000\) µm² (side about 224 µm) and the die to about \(264 \times 264 \approx 69\,500\) µm², some 11 % less silicon, but with much less room for wires.

The aspect ratio changes the shape but not the core area. With the aspect ratio \(r\) = height ÷ width and core area \(A\), the width is \(\sqrt{A/r}\) and the height \(\sqrt{A\,r}\).

docs.title: 3.4 Power planning: the distribution network
docs.text:
Every cell needs VDD and VSS. Power planning builds a robust metal network, before placement, so that current reaches every corner of the core with as little voltage lost on the way as possible. This is the power distribution network (PDN), and it has four layers of structure (Figure 3.3).

Figure 3.3 Rings, straps, rails and vias. A schematic of the PDN: concentric VDD and VSS rings around the core, a mesh of vertical and horizontal straps on upper metal, thin rails along every row, and a via stack joining the levels. Element Layer Role Power rings wide upper metal around the core edge two or more concentric rings carry VDD and VSS round the block; everything taps off them Straps (stripes) thick upper metals (for example met4 and met5) wide vertical and horizontal wires crossing the core, forming a mesh that spreads the current evenly Standard-cell rails met1 thin horizontal VDD and VSS rails along every row; cells connect their power pins here Vias and via stacks between all layers small metal plugs from one layer to the next that stitch the met1 rails up through the straps to the rings, so that current flows from the rings down into the cells

Table 3.3 The levels of the power network.

docs.title: Why the grid must be strong
docs.text:
Two physical effects set the requirements.

IR drop is the voltage lost across the resistance of the power metal, \(V = I \times R\). If the grid is too thin, a cell far from the ring sees a sagging supply. In the course's example a cell might see 0.75 V where the supply is 0.80 V, a sag of 0.05 V or 6.25 %. Such a cell switches more slowly, which can break timing, so IR drop must be kept within a budget of a few percent of VDD.

Electromigration (EM) is the gradual erosion of metal under sustained high current density: over years the atoms are pushed along the wire, which thins and finally breaks, and the chip dies in the field.

Both have the same cure: wider straps, more of them, more vias, and thick upper metal for the backbone. A strong grid is a reliability requirement and not a luxury.

docs.title: 3.5 Macros, halos, blockages and pins
docs.text:
Several devices keep cells out of places where they would do harm.

  • A halo is a guard band drawn around a hard macro in which no standard cells may be placed. It keeps the macro's pins reachable, leaves room to connect its power and reduces congestion at its edges.
  • A placement blockage is any region where cells are forbidden (hard blockage) or limited in density (soft or partial blockage). It is used to keep a routing channel open, to reserve space for buffers or to stay clear of sensitive circuits.
  • Pin planning places each input or output near the logic that uses it, shortening routes and easing timing. Power pins are spread around the edge so that current enters the ring from several sides.

When a block has several macros, how they are arranged shapes the whole floorplan.

Style Description When to use Channel macros separated by gaps through which wires and buffers pass flexible and easier to route, at a cost in area Abutted macros edge to edge with no gap saves area; needs careful pin alignment and power hook-up

Table 3.4 Two ways to arrange macros.

The general strategy is to place macros along the boundary, orient their pins towards the standard-cell area, group macros that talk to each other and always leave a halo. The aim is to keep the middle of the core one large, contiguous, routable sea of rows.

docs.title: 3.6 The real knobs: OpenLANE and OpenROAD
docs.text:
In the OpenLANE and Sky130 flow, floorplanning is driven by a handful of configuration variables, set in config.tcl (or config.json), and by OpenROAD commands. The most consequential are shown below.

# --- OpenLANE floorplan configuration (config.tcl) ---
set ::env(FP_CORE_UTIL)     45        ;# target core utilisation, % (start low)
set ::env(FP_ASPECT_RATIO)  1         ;# core height / width (1 = square)
set ::env(FP_SIZING)        relative  ;# 'relative': size the die from utilisation
set ::env(DIE_AREA)         "0 0 300 300" ;# used when FP_SIZING is 'absolute' (um)

# --- I/O pins ---
set ::env(FP_IO_MODE)       1         ;# equidistant pins around the die edge
set ::env(FP_IO_HMETAL)     met3      ;# layer for pins on horizontal edges
set ::env(FP_IO_VMETAL)     met2      ;# layer for pins on vertical edges

# --- macros and halo ---
set ::env(PL_MACRO_HALO)    "10 10"   ;# keep-out halo round macros, um

# --- power distribution network ---
set ::env(FP_PDN_VPITCH)    50        ;# vertical strap spacing, um
set ::env(FP_PDN_HPITCH)    50        ;# horizontal strap spacing, um
set ::env(FP_PDN_VWIDTH)    1.6       ;# strap width, um: wider means less IR drop
set ::env(FP_PDN_HWIDTH)    1.6
set ::env(FP_PDN_CORE_RING) 1         ;# build a VDD/VSS ring round the core

Under the hood OpenROAD runs the steps directly, which is useful to recognise when reading logs.

# --- what OpenLANE calls in OpenROAD ---
initialize_floorplan -utilization 45 -aspect_ratio 1 -site unithd   ;# rows, core and die
place_pins -hor_layers met3 -ver_layers met2                         ;# pins on the die edges
pdngen                                                               ;# rings + straps + rails

Lowering FP_CORE_UTIL spreads the cells out (easier routing, a bigger die); raising it packs them (a smaller die, more congestion). FP_ASPECT_RATIO reshapes the core. The FP_PDN_* widths and pitches trade the robustness of the PDN (the IR-drop and EM margin) against the routing area that the straps consume. The flow also places well-tap cells in the rows; they appear again in Chapter 8 when electrical rules are checked.

Variable names

The variable names above are those of the classic OpenLANE flow. Names and defaults change between versions of OpenLANE, so check them against the documentation of the version you install (Chapter 9) before relying on them.

docs.title: 3.7 A common misconception
docs.text:
Common misconception

"Higher utilisation is always better, because the die is smaller and cheaper." Not so. Above the sweet spot congestion explodes: nets cannot find a legal route, the tool inserts detours and buffers that eat the whitespace you saved, timing degrades, and you burn days on failed routing iterations. A slightly larger die that closes on the first pass is almost always cheaper, in engineering time, than a maximally packed one that will not converge.

Think about it

You set utilisation to 85 % and routing fails with congestion hot spots near the SRAMs. What do you try first, and why?

Answer

Try a bigger halo first. The congestion is local to the macros, not global, so the cheapest cure is local too. If that is not enough, lower utilisation by a few points, add placement blockages to steer cells away from the macro pins, or change the aspect ratio so that the congested dimension has more routing tracks.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Floorplanning fixes die and core size, shape, pins, macro positions and the power grid; everything later lives inside it.
  • Cells sit in rows divided into sites; alternate rows are flipped so that they share rails.
  • Utilisation is cell area divided by core area; 60 to 75 % balances cost against routability.
  • Rings, straps, rails and vias form the power network; IR drop and electromigration require that it be strong.
  • Macros go to the edges with halos, and pins go near the logic that uses them. In OpenLANE the main levers are FP_CORE_UTIL, FP_ASPECT_RATIO, PL_MACRO_HALO and the FP_PDN_* variables.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 3.1: Size a block

A block has 50 000 cells of 2.5 µm² each, 62.5 % utilisation, a square core and a 10 µm margin. Find the core side and the die side.

Answer

Cell area \(= 50\,000 \times 2.5 = 125\,000\) µm². Core area \(= 125\,000 / 0.625 = 200\,000\) µm². Core side \(= \sqrt{200\,000} \approx 447\) µm. Die side \(= 447 + 2 \times 10 \approx 467\) µm.

Exercise 3.2: Square or tall?

A block has 35 000 cells averaging 3 µm², 65 % utilisation and a 15 µm margin. (a) Find the core side, die side and die area for a square core. (b) Repeat for an aspect ratio (height ÷ width) of 2. (c) Which shape uses less silicon, and why might you still choose the other?

Answer

(a) Cell area 105 000 µm²; core area \(105\,000 / 0.65 \approx 161\,538\) µm²; core side \(\approx 401.9\) µm; die side \(\approx 431.9\) µm; die area \(\approx 186\,550\) µm². (b) With the same core area, width \(= \sqrt{161\,538 / 2} \approx 284.2\) µm and height \(= 2 \times 284.2 = 568.4\) µm. The die is \(314.2 \times 598.4\) µm, about \(188\,000\) µm². (c) The square. For a fixed core area it has the shortest perimeter, so the margin costs least. A tall shape might still be chosen to fit a slot in a larger chip or to line up with pins.

Exercise 3.3: A slow cell in the middle

Cells in the middle of the chip are slower than identical cells near the edge. Which floorplan problem do you suspect, and what do you do?

Answer

IR drop: the supply sags far from the rings, so the cells there switch more slowly. Widen or add straps and add vias.

Exercise 3.4: Utilisation and die cost

For Example 3.1, compute the core area and the die side if utilisation is 60 % instead of 70 %. By how much does the die area grow compared with the 70 % case?

Answer

Core area \(= 40\,000 / 0.60 \approx 66\,667\) µm², side \(\approx 258.2\) µm. Die side \(= 258.2 + 40 = 298.2\) µm, die area \(\approx 88\,900\) µm². Compared with 77 800 µm² this is about 14 % more silicon, bought in exchange for more routing room.

Exercise 3.5: Why build the PDN first?

The power grid is built before placement, not afterwards. Give two reasons.

Answer

Standard cells can then snap straight onto the rails, and the placer and router know from the start which tracks and areas the straps occupy. Power also needs the best (thick, low-resistance) metal and the least flexibility; building it later would force it into whatever space the cells and signal wires had left over.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Antenna effect Damage to a thin gate oxide by charge that a long, still-unconnected metal wire collects from the plasma during fabrication. Cured by layer jumping or an antenna diode. See Chapter 6. ASIC Application-specific integrated circuit. In this book, a standard-cell ASIC built from a library of ready-made cells. ATPG Automatic test-pattern generation: computing the input vectors that expose manufacturing defects, usually under the stuck-at fault model. Blockage A region of the core where placement of cells is forbidden or density-limited. Buffer A cell that re-drives a signal without changing its logic value, used to break up long or heavily loaded nets or to add delay on a hold-critical path. Clock gating Switching the clock off to idle register banks to save power, using integrated clock-gate (ICG) cells. Clock-tree synthesis (CTS) Building a balanced, buffered network that delivers the clock to every flip-flop at nearly the same time. See Chapter 5. Clock uncertainty A margin subtracted from setup and hold slack for clock jitter and safety. Core The inner region of the die in which standard cells and macros are placed and routed. Corner A named combination of process, voltage and temperature at which cell delays are characterised: slow (SS), typical (TT) or fast (FF). CPPR (CRPR) Clock-path pessimism removal: crediting back pessimism counted twice on the part of the clock path that launch and capture share. Critical path The timing path with the smallest slack; it sets the maximum clock frequency. DEF Design Exchange Format: the file that records the placement and routing of a design. Density fill Non-functional dummy metal added after routing so that every window of every layer meets the foundry's minimum and maximum metal density. DFT Design for test: inserting structures, chiefly scan chains, that make a manufactured chip controllable and observable. Die The whole piece of silicon, edge to edge, including the margin around the core. DRC Design rule check: comparing every shape of the layout with the foundry's geometric rules. See Chapter 8. Drive strength The size of a cell's transistors, written _1, _2, _4 or ×1, ×2, ×4: bigger cells drive larger loads faster but cost area, power and input capacitance. Electromigration (EM) The slow erosion of metal under sustained high current density, which can finally open a wire. ERC Electrical rule check: finding floating gates, power-to-ground shorts, wrongly tied wells and missing taps. Floorplan The first physical stage: the die and core size, aspect ratio, pins, macro positions and the power grid. FPGA Field-programmable gate array: a reprogrammable fabric of look-up tables and other blocks. g-cell A coarse routing tile used by global routing and by congestion maps, many tracks wide. GDSII Graphic Design System II: the industry-standard binary stream format for a finished layout, pure geometry by layer. Halo A keep-out guard band around a hard macro in which no standard cells are placed. Hold time, hold slack The time for which data must stay steady after the clock edge, and the margin by which a path meets that requirement. Independent of the clock period. HPWL Half-perimeter wirelength: the width plus the height of the box enclosing all the pins of a net. IR drop The voltage lost across the resistance of the power grid, \(V = I \times R\). Latency (insertion delay) The delay from the clock source to a flip-flop's clock pin. LEC Logic equivalence checking: a formal proof that two designs, such as the RTL and the final netlist, compute the same function. LEF Library Exchange Format: the physical abstract of cells (outline, pins, blockages) and the technology (metal layers, vias, rules). Legalisation The placement phase that removes overlaps and snaps cells to rows and sites. Liberty (.lib) The characterised timing and power model of a cell library, one file per corner. LVS Layout versus schematic: extracting a netlist from the layout and proving that it matches the intended netlist. MCMM Multi-corner multi-mode analysis: timing every functional mode at every relevant corner. Net The logical connection of a set of pins in a netlist. The physical metal that realises it is its wire. OASIS Open Artwork System Interchange Standard: a compact successor to GDSII. OCV On-chip variation: the small differences between nominally identical cells on one die, modelled by derating. OpenLANE The open-source orchestrator that runs Yosys, OpenROAD, Magic, KLayout and netgen as one RTL-to-GDSII flow. PDK Process design kit: a foundry's design rules, device models, layer definitions and standard-cell library for one process. PDN Power distribution network: the rings, straps, rails and vias that carry VDD and VSS to every cell. Pitch The centre-to-centre distance between neighbouring routing tracks. PPA Power, performance, area: the three goals that pull against one another. PVT Process, voltage and temperature: the three variables that set a cell's delay. RTL Register-transfer level: a description of a circuit as registers and the logic between them. Scan chain Scan flip-flops linked into a shift register so that a tester can set and read every register. SDC Synopsys Design Constraints: the Tcl dialect that states clocks, input and output delays and timing exceptions. Setup time, setup slack The time for which data must be steady before the clock edge, and the margin by which a path meets its deadline. Depends on the clock period. Site The unit grid of a row; a cell's width is a whole number of sites. Skew The difference in clock arrival between two flip-flops: capture latency minus launch latency. Slack Required time minus arrival time. Negative slack is a violation. SPEF Standard Parasitic Exchange Format: the extracted resistance and capacitance of every net. Standard cell A pre-designed, pre-characterised logic gate of fixed height that the flow places in rows. STA Static timing analysis: exhaustive, vector-less checking of every timing path. Streaming out Writing the final layout as a GDSII or OASIS file. Tapeout The moment the final mask data is sent to the foundry. Timing arc A characterised delay from one input pin to one output pin of a cell, tabulated against input slew and output load. Timing closure Making every timing path meet its constraint at every corner and mode. TNS, WNS Total and worst negative slack: the sum of all negative slacks, and the single most negative one. Track A legal centre line for a wire on a routing layer. Utilisation Total standard-cell area divided by core area. Via A small metal plug joining a wire on one layer to a wire on the next. Wire-load model A statistical estimate of a net's capacitance from its fan-out, used before real wires exist.

docs.title: Chapter 2: Logic Synthesis and Timing Basics
docs.text:
Synthesis is the first stage at which an abstract piece of Verilog stops being an idea and starts becoming hardware. The tool reads the RTL, works out the Boolean logic and the registers that it describes, and maps that logic onto real building blocks, the standard cells of one manufacturing process, while squeezing timing, area and power to meet the constraints it has been given. The output is a gate-level netlist: the same design, now written entirely in NANDs, AOIs, flip-flops and buffers that a foundry can actually make.

Synthesis is also where timing first matters. A gate-level netlist is useful only if its gates are fast enough, so this chapter introduces, alongside the tool flow, the arithmetic of setup and hold slack that the rest of the book builds on.

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you can:

  1. Describe the three phases of synthesis and read a small gate-level netlist.
  2. Explain timing arcs and drive strengths in a cell library.
  3. Compute setup and hold slack for a register-to-register path, and find the critical path and the maximum clock frequency.
  4. Write basic SDC constraints and read a Yosys synthesis script.
  5. Explain scan chains and say what synthesis does and does not prove.

docs.title: 2.1 What synthesis does
docs.text:
RTL describes behaviour: "on the rising clock edge, sum becomes a + b". Logic synthesis turns that behaviour into a structural netlist, an interconnection of standard cells, that is logically equivalent to the RTL but can be built in silicon. Three conceptual phases happen inside the tool.

Elaboration. The RTL is parsed, parameters are resolved, generate loops are unrolled and the hierarchy is built. Behavioural constructs (+, *, if, case, always blocks) become a generic, technology-independent netlist of abstract gates and inferred registers. This representation is often called GTECH or, in Yosys, RTLIL. No real cell has been chosen yet.

Technology mapping. Each generic gate and register is replaced by a real cell from the target .lib: a sky130_fd_sc_hd__nand2_1, a __dfrtp_2 flip-flop and so on. This is where an abstract AND becomes "this exact NAND followed by this inverter, with these delays".

Optimisation. The tool restructures the logic, resizes cells, inserts buffers and shares common sub-expressions until timing is met with as little area and power as possible. Optimisation is interleaved with mapping; modern engines such as ABC map and optimise together.

docs.title: Before and after
docs.text:
Consider a registered 4-bit adder.

module add_reg (input clk, input [3:0] a, b, output reg [4:0] sum);
  always @(posedge clk)
    sum <= a + b;      // 4-bit + 4-bit -> 5-bit, registered
endmodule

After synthesis the + is gone. In its place are XOR, AND and AOI-style cells forming the carry logic, and each bit of sum has a D flip-flop. The fragment below is a schematic of that result, simplified and with the carry chain elided, to show its character; a real run produces a longer netlist with different cell choices.

module add_reg (clk, a, b, sum);
  input clk;  input [3:0] a, b;  output [4:0] sum;
  wire n1, n2, n3, c0, c1, c2, c3;

  // the lowest bit of the adder, mapped to real cells
  sky130_fd_sc_hd__xor2_1   U1 (.A(a[0]), .B(b[0]), .X(n1));
  sky130_fd_sc_hd__and2_1   U2 (.A(a[0]), .B(b[0]), .X(c0));
  sky130_fd_sc_hd__o21ai_1  U3 (.A1(a[1]), .A2(b[1]), .B1(c0), .Y(n2));
  // ... the carry chain continues for bits 1 to 3 ...

  // registers: one D flip-flop per sum bit
  sky130_fd_sc_hd__dfrtp_1  Q0 (.CLK(clk), .D(n1), .Q(sum[0]));
  sky130_fd_sc_hd__dfrtp_1  Q1 (.CLK(clk), .D(n2), .Q(sum[1]));
  // ... Q2, Q3, Q4 ...
endmodule

Notice what changed. The arithmetic operator vanished, replaced by explicit cells; the reg became five concrete dfrtp (rising-edge D flip-flop with reset) cells; and every wire is now a named net that will become a physical wire.

The lowest bit of a + b is a half adder: the sum bit is a XOR b and the carry is a AND b. Each of those two gates is one standard cell, xor2_1 and and2_1.

Definition: standard cell

A standard cell is a pre-designed, pre-characterised, fixed-height logic primitive (inverter, NAND, AOI, flip-flop, buffer) that the foundry guarantees it can manufacture. Synthesis's whole job is to express the design using only cells from the chosen library.

docs.title: 2.2 Inputs and outputs
docs.text:
Synthesis is a function of three inputs and produces one primary output together with some reports.

Role File What it provides Input: design RTL .v, .sv, .vhd the behaviour: modules, always blocks, arithmetic Input: library .lib (Liberty) the cells available, with timing, power and area characterised for the process Input: constraints .sdc clock period, input and output delays, false paths: the goals the netlist must meet Output: netlist gate-level .v structural Verilog instantiating library cells and nets Output: reports timing, area and power logs worst slack, cell count, total area, estimated power

Table 2.1 What synthesis reads and writes.

docs.title: 2.3 Inside the cell library
docs.text:
The .lib file is the tool's model of reality. For every cell it stores the logic function, the area, the power and, above all for synthesis, the timing arcs.

A timing arc is a measured delay from one input pin to one output pin of a cell, for example from A to Y of a NAND2. The delay is not a single number. It depends on two things, and the library stores it as a two-dimensional look-up table (a non-linear delay model, NLDM):

  • How fast the input changes. A slowly rising input, one with a large slew, makes the cell respond later.
  • How much the cell has to drive. Every input that the output feeds adds capacitance, and more load means a slower output.

(An analogy: how long it takes to fill buckets depends on how quickly the tap opens and how many buckets are waiting.)

For flip-flops the library also stores setup and hold constraint arcs: the data must be stable before the clock edge (setup) and for a while after it (hold). Violating either corrupts the captured value. The input capacitance of each pin is the load that the pin presents to whatever drives it, so a net's fan-out slows its driver by the sum of the pins it feeds.

docs.title: Drive strength
docs.text:
The same logic function is offered in several strengths. The suffix _1, _2, _4 (or X1, X2, X4) denotes the size of the transistors.

Cell Drive Delay into a big load Area Load it puts on its driver nand2_1 ×1 slow small small nand2_2 ×2 faster bigger bigger nand2_4 ×4 fastest biggest biggest

Table 2.2 Drive strength trades speed against area, power and input load.

Cell selection and sizing is a core synthesis decision. A lightly loaded net gets a ×1 cell; a net that feeds many gates or a long wire gets a ×2 or ×4 cell or a buffer chain. Up-sizing cuts delay but costs area and power.

Think about it

If ×4 is always faster, why not make every cell ×4?

Answer

A bigger cell has bigger inputs, which slow down whatever drives it, and it leaks more power. Up-sizing one gate therefore slows the gate before it, and doing it everywhere burns leakage everywhere. Sizing is a balance, not a maximisation.

docs.title: 2.4 Timing basics
docs.text: Synthesis optimises for speed, so we first need to say exactly what "fast enough" means.

docs.title: A path from one flip-flop to the next
docs.text:
A synchronous design is made of registers separated by clouds of combinational logic. Figure 2.1 shows one such path. On a clock edge the launch flip-flop sends out a new value. The value must cross the logic and settle at the capture flip-flop before the next edge, but it must not disturb what the capture flip-flop is taking in on the current edge.

Figure 2.1 A register-to-register path. A launch flip-flop, a cloud of combinational logic and a capture flip-flop, all clocked by the same clock.

docs.title: Three numbers from every flip-flop
docs.text:
• Clock-to-Q (\(t_{cq}\)): after the clock edge, how long until the new value appears at output Q.
  • Setup time (\(t_{su}\)): how long the input must be steady before the clock edge to be captured reliably.
  • Hold time (\(t_{h}\)): how long the input must stay steady after the clock edge.

(A photographer's flash is a good picture: you must be in position a moment before it fires, which is setup, and keep still a moment after, which is hold, or the picture blurs.)

docs.title: The setup check: is it too slow?
docs.text:
Data launched at the clock edge arrives at the capture flip-flop after clock-to-Q plus the delay of the slowest route through the logic. It is required there by the next edge, one clock period \(T\) later, less the setup time. The difference is the slack:

\[\text{setup slack} = (T - t_{su}) - (t_{cq} + t_{logic,max})\]

Positive slack means time to spare; negative slack is a violation, and the chip fails at this clock rate. Figure 2.2 shows the numbers of the next example on a time line.

Example 2.1: Setup slack at two clock periods

A path has \(t_{cq} = 0.40\) ns, slowest logic \(3.20\) ns and \(t_{su} = 0.30\) ns.

  1. At \(T = 5.0\) ns: the data arrives at \(0.40 + 3.20 = 3.60\) ns. It is required by \(5.0 - 0.30 = 4.70\) ns. Slack \(= 4.70 - 3.60 = +1.10\) ns. The check is met, with 1.1 ns to spare.
  2. At \(T = 3.5\) ns: the requirement is \(3.5 - 0.30 = 3.20\) ns, so slack \(= 3.20 - 3.60 = -0.40\) ns. The check fails: the clock has outrun the logic.
Figure 2.2 Setup slack on a time line. A time line for the example: clock-to-Q and slowest logic bring the data to 3.60 ns; the data is required by 4.70 ns, which is the next edge at 5.0 ns less the 0.30 ns setup time; the slack is 1.10 ns.

docs.title: The hold check: is it too fast?
docs.text:
The same clock edge that launches a new value also captures the old one at the downstream flip-flop. If the new value races through a very short path it can arrive while the capture flip-flop is still holding on to the old one. So hold uses the fastest route through the logic:

\[\text{hold slack} = (t_{cq} + t_{logic,min}) - t_{h}\]

The clock period \(T\) does not appear in this formula. Slowing the clock therefore does not fix a hold problem.

Example 2.2: Hold slack

With \(t_{cq} = 0.40\), fastest logic \(0.30\) and \(t_h = 0.15\) ns:

\[0.40 + 0.30 - 0.15 = +0.55 \text{ ns}\]

The check is met. Now connect the two flip-flops almost directly, with a fast flip-flop having \(t_{cq} = 0.10\) ns and no logic at all:

\[0.10 + 0 - 0.15 = -0.05 \text{ ns}\]

The check fails. This is the classic hold-critical topology: a flip-flop feeding another flip-flop with nothing in between.

docs.title: The critical path and the maximum clock
docs.text:
A design has thousands or millions of such paths. The one with the least slack is the critical path. It alone fixes the fastest possible clock:

\[f_{max} = \frac{1}{t_{cq} + t_{logic,max} + t_{su}}\]

For the numbers of Example 2.1, \(f_{max} = 1 / (0.40 + 3.20 + 0.30\ \text{ns}) = 1 / 3.9\ \text{ns} \approx 256\) MHz. Synthesis spends its effort here: restructuring and up-sizing cells on the critical path, and saving area and power everywhere else.

Experiment: break setup, then hold

In the course's interactive calculator you could shrink \(T\) until setup fails, and then shrink the fastest logic towards zero and watch hold fail while noting that changing \(T\) does nothing for it. You can do the same on paper with Examples 2.1 and 2.2: re-evaluate setup for \(T = 4.0, 3.9, 3.8\) ns and hold for fastest-logic delays of \(0.30, 0.20, 0.10, 0\) ns.

docs.title: 2.5 Constraints: telling the tool the goal
docs.text:
Without a clock period, "make it fast" means nothing: the tool has no idea how fast the clock runs or when signals arrive. SDC (Synopsys Design Constraints) is a dialect of Tcl, understood by every tool in the flow, that says it. Synthesis, layout and timing analysis all read the same file.

# --- the clock: 10 ns period = 100 MHz, 50 % duty ---
create_clock -name clk -period 10.0 [get_ports clk]

# --- inputs arrive 2 ns after the edge; outputs are needed 3 ns before the next one ---
set_input_delay  -clock clk 2.0 [all_inputs]
set_output_delay -clock clk 3.0 [all_outputs]

# --- a hard cap on one path, independent of any clock ---
set_max_delay 4.0 -from [get_pins U1/A] -to [get_pins U9/Y]

# --- a configuration pin that never changes in operation: do not time it ---
set_false_path -from [get_ports test_mode]

# --- a slow multiplier is allowed two cycles ---
set_multicycle_path 2 -setup -from [get_pins mul/*] -to [get_pins acc_reg/D]
set_multicycle_path 1 -hold  -from [get_pins mul/*] -to [get_pins acc_reg/D]

# --- the world outside: what drives our inputs, what our outputs drive ---
set_driving_cell -lib_cell sky130_fd_sc_hd__inv_2 [all_inputs]
set_load 0.05 [all_outputs]            ;# 50 fF on each output
Command What it does create_clock defines a clock's period (hence frequency), waveform and source port; the metronome every setup and hold check is measured against set_input_delay models how late data arrives at an input, relative to the clock: how much of the period is already used before the signal reaches the block set_output_delay models how early an output must be valid so the next block can capture it: how much of the period the next block needs after ours set_max_delay an explicit upper bound on one path's delay, independent of any clock; useful for combinational or asynchronous interfaces set_false_path marks a path that exists in the wiring but is never exercised (for example a static configuration pin); the tool stops optimising and reporting it set_multicycle_path relaxes a path that legitimately takes more than one clock cycle to settle, so that it is not flagged as a violation set_driving_cell, set_load model the real neighbours, so delays at the edges of the block are realistic rather than ideal

Table 2.3 The essential SDC commands.

Constraints are part of the design

A false path that you declare wrongly is never checked, and can fail on silicon. Constraints must be reviewed with the same care as code.

docs.title: 2.6 Optimisation: moving along the PPA curve
docs.text:
Synthesis is a constrained optimisation over the three axes of PPA (Section 1.6). The constraints pin down "meet 100 MHz", and the tool then minimises area and power subject to that. Its main levers are:

  • Restructuring: re-factoring the Boolean network, for instance turning a deep chain of gates into a balanced tree, to cut logic depth on the critical path.
  • Sizing: swapping a cell for a stronger (×4) or weaker (×1) variant, trading delay against area and power. Cells with spare slack are down-sized.
  • Buffering and cloning: inserting buffers on long or high-fan-out nets, or duplicating a driver, so that a single overloaded cell does not dominate a path.
  • Multi-threshold libraries: when a library offers cells of several threshold voltages, low-leakage (high-threshold) cells can be used off the critical path and fast (low-threshold) cells only where they are needed.

Example 2.3: The same adder at opposite ends of the curve

A 32-bit adder built as a ripple-carry chain has about 32 gate delays and a tiny area. It is too slow for a 500 MHz clock. A carry-lookahead (prefix) adder has about 6 gate delays and meets timing, but costs roughly twice the area and more power. The function is identical; the constraints decide which structure the tool builds.

Tighten the clock of a block from 10 ns to 8 ns and re-synthesise. Timing now passes, but the area report may jump by 20 % and power rises too. Nothing about the function changed: the tool up-sized cells, added buffers and restructured logic to buy 2 ns, and paid for it in silicon and switching energy. You moved along the PPA curve; nothing came free.

docs.title: 2.7 A synthesis script in Yosys
docs.text:
Yosys is the open-source synthesis engine at the heart of OpenLANE. A minimal, explicit script (what the one-line synth macro expands to, in outline) shows each step.

# run with:  yosys -s synth.ys
read_verilog add_reg.v                  # 1. parse the RTL into RTLIL
hierarchy -check -top add_reg           # 2. choose the top module, elaborate the hierarchy
proc                                    # 3. always blocks, if and case -> logic + flip-flops
opt                                     # 4. constant-fold, remove dead logic, simplify
fsm; opt                                #    (optional) extract and optimise state machines
memory; opt                             #    (optional) map memories to logic or block RAM
techmap; opt                            # 5. map generic operators to gate-level primitives
dfflibmap -liberty sky130_fd_sc_hd.lib  # 6. map generic flip-flops to library flip-flops
abc -liberty sky130_fd_sc_hd.lib        # 7. map and optimise combinational logic to cells
clean                                   #    drop unused wires and cells
write_verilog -noattr add_reg_netlist.v # 8. write the gate-level netlist
Command Role in the flow read_verilog parses the RTL into Yosys's internal representation, RTLIL hierarchy -top names the top module and elaborates the module tree; -check reports missing modules proc converts behavioural always blocks (if, case, assignments) into multiplexer logic and inferred flip-flops opt generic clean-up: constant propagation, dead-code removal, trivial simplification; run repeatedly between other passes techmap maps coarse operators (adders, muxes, shifts) down to a generic gate-level library dfflibmap maps the generic flip-flops onto real sequential cells of the given .lib, matching their set, reset and enable flavours abc -liberty hands the combinational logic to ABC, which maps and optimises it for timing and area against the Liberty cells write_verilog writes the structural netlist; -noattr strips internal attributes for a clean file

Table 2.4 The steps of a minimal Yosys script.

Think about it

Why are dfflibmap (sequential) and abc (combinational) separate steps?

Answer

Flip-flops must map to specific library cells with matching reset and enable pins, which ABC's combinational optimiser does not reason about. Yosys therefore pins the flip-flops down first, and then lets ABC reshape freely only the cloud of logic between them.

docs.title: 2.8 Making chips testable: scan
docs.text:
Factories make defects. Every manufactured chip must be tested, but a register buried deep inside the design cannot be reached from the pins. Design for test (DFT) makes the netlist controllable and observable, and its workhorse is scan.

  • Scan flip-flops. Each ordinary D flip-flop is replaced by a scan flip-flop with an extra multiplexer on its D input. In functional mode it behaves normally; in scan mode it takes its data from the previous flip-flop's output.
  • Scan chains. The scan flip-flops are linked into long shift registers (Figure 2.3). In test mode the tester shifts in any state it likes, runs one functional clock, and shifts the result out.
  • ATPG (automatic test-pattern generation) computes the input vectors that expose defects, typically under the stuck-at fault model in which each node is stuck at 0 or at 1.
  • Fault coverage is the fraction of modelled faults that the patterns detect. Production chips aim well above 95 to 99 %; a low figure lets defective parts reach customers.
Figure 2.3 A scan chain. Three scan flip-flops joined into a shift register: each takes D from its own logic in functional mode and SI from its neighbour in test mode.

Scan insertion happens during or after synthesis. The extra multiplexer costs a little area and a little timing, which is why DFT is budgeted into the flow from the start and not bolted on later.

docs.title: 2.9 What synthesis does not prove
docs.text:
Common misconception

"Synthesis ran without errors, so my design is correct." Synthesis only guarantees that the netlist does the same as the RTL you gave it, bugs included. If the RTL is wrong, the gates will be faithfully and efficiently wrong.

Three different activities must not be confused. Verification (simulation, formal proofs) checks that the RTL does what you intended. Equivalence checking (LEC) proves that the netlist still matches the RTL after optimisation. Synthesis is neither of these.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Synthesis elaborates the RTL, maps it onto real library cells and optimises for PPA: RTL plus .lib plus .sdc gives a gate-level netlist.
  • The .lib gives timing arcs (tables of delay against input slew and output load), setup and hold requirements and drive strengths; sizing is a balance, not a maximum.
  • Setup slack is \((T - t_{su}) - (t_{cq} + t_{logic,max})\). Hold slack is \((t_{cq} + t_{logic,min}) - t_h\) and does not depend on \(T\). The critical path sets \(f_{max}\).
  • SDC states the goals (create_clock, input and output delays, false and multicycle paths); a Yosys script runs proc, opt, techmap, dfflibmap, abc and write_verilog.
  • Scan chains make the manufactured chip testable. Synthesis preserves the logic; it does not check that the logic is right.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 2.1: Slack by hand

A path has \(t_{cq} = 0.3\) ns, slowest logic \(6.2\) ns, fastest logic \(0.1\) ns, \(t_{su} = 0.2\) ns, \(t_h = 0.25\) ns, and the clock is 7 ns. (a) What is the setup slack? (b) What is the hold slack? (c) Would a 10 ns clock fix either problem?

Answer

(a) \((7 - 0.2) - (0.3 + 6.2) = 6.8 - 6.5 = +0.3\) ns, met. (b) \((0.3 + 0.1) - 0.25 = +0.15\) ns, met. (c) Neither fails. But note that a longer clock could only ever help setup; hold does not depend on the period.

Exercise 2.2: Maximum frequency

For the path of Exercise 2.1, what is the maximum clock frequency?

Answer

\(f_{max} = 1 / (0.3 + 6.2 + 0.2\ \text{ns}) = 1 / 6.7\ \text{ns} \approx 149\) MHz. At 7 ns (143 MHz) the path has 0.3 ns of slack, which is exactly \(7 - 6.7\).

Exercise 2.3: Reading an SDC file

Explain in words what each of these lines does.

create_clock -name clk -period 8.0 [get_ports clk]
set_input_delay -clock clk 1.5 [all_inputs]
set_false_path -from [get_ports scan_en]
Answer

The first defines a clock named clk on port clk with an 8 ns period (125 MHz). The second says that every input arrives 1.5 ns after the clock edge, so only \(8 - 1.5 = 6.5\) ns of the period remains for logic between an input and its capture register (less setup). The third tells the tool to ignore all timing paths starting at scan_en, so they are neither optimised nor reported. It is safe only if that signal really never matters to timing in operation.

Exercise 2.4: Which half of the check fails?

A register-to-register path has \(t_{cq} = 0.35\) ns, slowest logic 4.10 ns, fastest logic 0.20 ns, \(t_{su} = 0.25\) ns and \(t_h = 0.10\) ns. At \(T = 5.0\) ns, compute the setup slack, the hold slack and \(f_{max}\).

Answer

Setup: \((5.0 - 0.25) - (0.35 + 4.10) = 4.75 - 4.45 = +0.30\) ns. Hold: \((0.35 + 0.20) - 0.10 = +0.45\) ns. \(f_{max} = 1 / (0.35 + 4.10 + 0.25\ \text{ns}) = 1 / 4.70\ \text{ns} \approx 213\) MHz.

Exercise 2.5: Why scan costs timing

Why does replacing every flip-flop by a scan flip-flop add a little delay to the design, and why is that accepted?

Answer

Each scan flip-flop has a multiplexer in front of D, which adds a small delay (and area) to every register-to-register path that ends there. It is accepted because without scan a manufactured chip cannot be tested thoroughly, so defective parts would reach customers; the cost is planned for in the timing budget.

Exercise 2.6: The 10 ns to 8 ns experiment

You tighten the clock from 10 ns to 8 ns and re-synthesise. Timing passes, but area is up 20 % and power is up too. The RTL is unchanged. Explain.

Answer

To save 2 ns on the critical path the tool up-sized cells, added buffers and restructured logic. All of these cost area and switching energy. You moved along the PPA curve rather than getting something for free.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Physical Verification and Tapeout
docs.text:
Routing is done, the parasitics are extracted and timing looks green. But a layout cannot be sent to a factory on optimism. Signoff is the final gate: a battery of exacting, tool-driven checks, all of which must come back clean before the layout is streamed out. A single unresolved violation can cost a full mask set and a delay of months, so the rule is simple: everything must be clean before tapeout.

This chapter walks through every check in turn (design rules, layout versus schematic, antenna, electrical rules, density, IR drop, electromigration and formal equivalence), then explains what a GDSII file actually is, what the foundry does with it, and what the tapeout checklist looks like.

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you can:

  1. Name the signoff checks and say what each one catches.
  2. Explain design rule checking, read a DRC report and apply a simple rule by hand.
  3. Explain layout-versus-schematic checking, and why a DRC-clean layout can still be wrong.
  4. Describe antenna, ERC and density-fill checks, IR drop and electromigration signoff, and equivalence checking.
  5. Describe GDSII and OASIS, the foundry's use of them, and the tapeout checklist.

docs.title: 8.1 What signoff means
docs.text:
Signoff is the last stage of physical design: the point at which the team formally certifies that the layout is correct, manufacturable and meets its specification. Every earlier stage optimised, using fast, approximate engines; signoff verifies, using slow, exact "golden" engines and the full set of corners. It is normal for a design that passed optimisation to reveal a handful of signoff violations that must then be fixed.

Check The question it answers Open-source tool Static timing (STA) does every path meet setup and hold, at every corner and mode? OpenSTA DRC does the geometry obey the foundry's manufacturing rules? Magic, KLayout LVS does the layout implement exactly the intended netlist? netgen Power: IR drop, electromigration is the supply strong enough everywhere, and for years? OpenROAD Equivalence (LEC) is the final netlist still logically identical to the RTL? Yosys eqy

Table 8.1 The main signoff checks. Commercial equivalents include PrimeTime, Calibre and Conformal.

Signal-integrity (crosstalk) analysis completes the list; it was introduced in Chapter 6 and is run with the post-route parasitics.

docs.title: 8.2 DRC: can it be built?
docs.text:
A design rule check compares every shape of the layout with the foundry's design rule manual, a long list of geometric constraints that guarantee the shapes can be manufactured. Chips are printed with light through masks, and then etched. Draw two wires too close and the light blurs them into one, or the etch bridges them. Every rule traces back to a physical limit: the optical resolution of the stepper, the flatness that polishing can achieve, etch loading. The manual is the foundry's contract: obey it and the foundry guarantees its yield; break it and it will not even accept the mask data.

The rules fall into families: minimum width, minimum spacing, enclosure and overlap (metal must extend past a via by a minimum amount), minimum area, via rules, and density (each layer must hold between a minimum and a maximum fraction of metal in any window, Section 8.4).

Rule Layer Meaning Minimum (simplified) met1.1 metal 1 width 0.14 µm met1.2 metal 1 spacing 0.14 µm met1.6 metal 1 area 0.083 µm² via.1 via 1 exact via size 0.15 × 0.15 µm via.4 metal 1 enclosure of a via 0.055 µm poly.2 poly spacing 0.21 µm

Table 8.2 Illustrative rules in a Sky130-style process. The values are simplified for teaching; always use the foundry's own rule manual for real work.

Figure 8.1 A spacing rule: clean and violating. Two metal-1 wires 0.20 µm wide: with a gap of 0.14 µm they are clean; with a gap of 0.10 µm they violate rule met1.2 and may print as one wire.

Example 8.1: Applying the rules by hand

A spacing check. Two parallel metal-1 wires are drawn 0.20 µm wide and 0.10 µm apart. The width, 0.20 µm, is above the 0.14 µm minimum (met1.1 is satisfied), but the spacing, 0.10 µm, is below the 0.14 µm minimum: met1.2 is violated. Moving the wires to 0.14 µm apart makes the layout clean.

An area check. A metal-1 rectangle is 0.14 µm wide and 0.50 µm long. The width is exactly the minimum. Its area is \(0.14 \times 0.50 = 0.070\) µm², below the 0.083 µm² minimum: met1.6 is violated. The rectangle must be lengthened to at least \(0.083 / 0.14 \approx 0.593\) µm.

Running DRC in Magic on the open-source flow looks like this.

# In the Magic console: load the layout, then check the whole cell
load user_proj_example
drc euclidean on
drc check
drc catchup
puts "DRC errors: [drc list count]"
drc why            ;# explain the error under the cursor box

The report lists each violation by rule name and place, so that you can zoom straight to it. You read it from the top, fix the biggest clusters first, and iterate until the total is exactly zero.

Metal1 spacing < 0.14um (met1.2)
  ( 12.480  8.210 ) ( 12.615  8.470 )
Via1 enclosure by Metal1 < 0.055um (via.4)
  ( 30.010 15.220 ) ( 30.160 15.375 )
Metal2 minimum area (met2.6)
  ( 44.900 22.100 ) ( 45.010 22.190 )
Total DRC errors found: 3

Each entry gives the rule, a human-readable description and the coordinates of a bounding box. "Clean" means a total of exactly 0.

docs.title: 8.3 LVS: is it the right circuit?
docs.text:
DRC proves that the layout can be built; it says nothing about whether it is correct. That is the work of layout versus schematic (LVS), which asks whether the physical layout implements exactly the circuit that the netlist describes. It has two halves.

  1. Extract. A tool reads the layout shapes, recognises every transistor and other device layer by layer, and traces the metal and vias to build a netlist from the layout.
  2. Compare. The extracted netlist is matched, device by device and net by net, against the source netlist, the one that was meant to be built. LVS declares a match only when devices agree in type, count and parameters (width and length within tolerance) and the nets joining them form the same graph.

LVS catches what DRC cannot see:

  • shorts: two nets that should be separate are touching;
  • opens: one net is broken into two;
  • wrong connections: a pin on the wrong net, a swapped device, a missing tie-off.

In the open-source flow Magic extracts and netgen compares.

# 1) Magic: extract a SPICE netlist from the layout
extract all
ext2spice lvs
ext2spice -o user_proj_example.spice

# 2) netgen: compare the layout netlist with the source netlist
netgen -batch lvs \
  "user_proj_example.spice user_proj_example" \
  "user_proj_example.v      user_proj_example" \
  $PDK_ROOT/sky130A/libs.tech/netgen/sky130A_setup.tcl \
  lvs.report

Circuit 1 contains 1842 devices, Circuit 2 contains 1842 devices.
Circuit 1 contains 2013 nets,    Circuit 2 contains 2013 nets.
Netlists match uniquely.
Result: Circuits match uniquely.

"Circuits match uniquely" is the phrase to hunt for. Anything else, such as unmatched nets, property errors or differing device counts, must be resolved before signoff.

Common misconception

"DRC-clean means my chip works." DRC only proves that the shapes are manufacturable; it is blind to connectivity. A layout can be 100 % DRC clean and still short two power rails together or leave a clock net floating. Only LVS, together with the electrical and antenna checks, confirms that the layout is the right circuit. You need all of them green.

docs.title: 8.4 Antenna, ERC and density fill
docs.text:
Antenna checks. As explained in Chapter 6, a large piece of connected metal can collect plasma charge during fabrication and rupture a thin gate oxide. The antenna rule limits the ratio of connected metal area to the gate area it drives. Signoff verifies every gate and every layer; diodes or layer jumps are inserted where a ratio is exceeded.

ERC, the electrical rule check, finds electrical mistakes that are legal geometry but broken circuits: floating gates, unconnected inputs, power-to-ground shorts, wells tied to the wrong supply, missing substrate or well taps. It is a cheap sanity net that catches connectivity blunders early.

Density fill. Each metal layer is polished flat, but polishing removes more material where metal is sparse and less where it is dense, leaving dips that harm the layers above. To keep density uniform, the tools scatter non-functional dummy metal fill shapes into empty regions so that every window on every layer falls inside the foundry's density band. Fill is added after routing and is deliberately connected to nothing.

docs.title: 8.5 Power signoff: IR drop and electromigration
docs.text:
IR drop. Current through the resistance of the power grid makes the local supply sag, \(V = I \times R\). IR-drop signoff simulates the grid under realistic switching activity and checks that the worst droop stays within the budget, commonly a few percent of VDD. Fixes are wider straps, more vias between grid layers or on-chip decoupling capacitance.

Electromigration (EM). High current density pushes metal atoms along a wire over time, thinning it until it opens, or bulging it until it shorts a neighbour. EM signoff checks that the average and peak current density in every wire and via stay below the foundry's limit for the target lifetime. Power and clock nets, which carry the most current, are the usual offenders; the fix is again wider metal and more vias.

IR drop and EM are two sides of the same coin: both are about current in the power grid. IR drop is the instantaneous voltage problem (a droop right now slows a cell); EM is the long-term reliability problem (sustained current wears the wire out over years). Widening a strap and adding vias helps both, which is why a robust grid designed in Chapter 3 pays off all the way to signoff.

docs.title: 8.6 Equivalence checking
docs.text:
By the time the netlist reaches signoff it has been through synthesis, scan insertion, clock-buffer insertion and late edits (ECOs). How do we know that it still does what the original RTL specified? Logic equivalence checking (LEC) is a formal, exhaustive proof, not a simulation, that the final gate-level netlist is logically identical to the RTL. It compares the two designs' Boolean functions at every state and output, and if they diverge it reports a counter-example input. Because the method is formal, a pass is a mathematical guarantee and not a sample. In the open-source world Yosys's eqy plays this role; commercially it is Conformal or Formality.

# Yosys-based equivalence check: RTL (gold) versus final netlist (gate)
eqy -f equiv.eqy
# ... partitions proven ...
# Successfully proved designs equivalent

docs.title: 8.7 GDSII, OASIS and tapeout
docs.text:
When every check is green the layout is exported in a form the foundry can use. The classic format is GDSII, a binary, hierarchical description of pure geometry. It knows nothing of logic; it is a database of shapes:

  • cells (structures): named groups of shapes that can refer to other cells, so a full chip is one top cell referring to thousands of standard-cell definitions;
  • polygons and paths: the shapes themselves;
  • layer and datatype numbers: which mask each shape belongs to (metal 1, poly, via), mapping the geometry onto the foundry's process layers.

OASIS is the modern successor: the same idea, often ten times smaller and faster to process. Writing either file is called streaming out, and a GDSII file is also called a stream file. KLayout and Magic read and write both.

# Magic: stream out the top cell to GDSII
load user_proj_example
gds write user_proj_example.gds

# KLayout: convert between formats in batch, or simply open the GDS to inspect layers
klayout -zz -rd input=user_proj_example.gds \
        -rd output=user_proj_example.oas \
        -r strmrun.rb

At the foundry the data goes through mask data preparation (splitting shapes into mask-writer figures and applying optical-proximity correction) and is written onto a set of photomasks, one or more per layer. In the fab a stepper shines light through each mask to pattern photoresist on the wafer (photolithography); etching, deposition, implantation and polishing then build that layer physically. The sequence repeats for every layer; then the wafer is diced, the dice are packaged and tested, and silicon exists (Figure 8.2).

Figure 8.2 What the foundry does with the file. Six steps from the GDSII or OASIS file through mask data preparation, photomasks, lithography, etch deposit and polish repeated for every layer, to dicing, packaging and testing.

Tapeout is the moment the final data is sent. The word dates from the time when layouts travelled to the factory on reels of magnetic tape.

docs.title: 8.8 The tapeout checklist
docs.text:
Before anyone writes the GDSII, every item below must be green.

Check Condition Timing (STA) setup and hold met on every path, all corners and modes; no negative slack DRC 0 violations against the foundry rule manual LVS "circuits match uniquely": no shorts, opens or device mismatches Antenna all antenna ratios within limits (diodes or jumpers inserted where needed) ERC no floating gates, no power-ground shorts; wells and taps correct Density every layer inside its minimum and maximum density band (fill added) IR drop worst-case supply droop within budget Electromigration current density under the limit for the target lifetime Crosstalk noise and delay change within margin Equivalence final netlist formally equivalent to the RTL Test scan chains verified; coverage target met

Table 8.3 The tapeout signoff checklist: all must be green.

Signoff is not a rubber stamp

It routinely finds real problems that the faster optimisation engines missed: a stray antenna violation, a hold failure at a corner, an IR-drop hot spot. Budget real schedule for signoff-and-fix iterations; treating signoff as a formality is how respins happen.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Signoff re-checks everything with exact engines, and every check must be clean.
  • DRC: the geometry obeys the foundry's rules. LVS: the layout's extracted netlist matches the intended one. They look at different things, and each is blind to what the other catches.
  • Antenna, ERC and density fill, IR drop and electromigration, and formal equivalence complete the list.
  • GDSII (or OASIS) is pure geometry by layer; the foundry turns it into masks and, layer by layer, into silicon. Sending it is the tapeout.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 8.1: Passes DRC, fails LVS

A layout passes DRC, but LVS reports two nets merged. What is wrong, and would the chip work?

Answer

A short: two wires that should be separate touch. The shapes are buildable, so DRC is happy, but the circuit is wrong and the chip would not work.

Exercise 8.2: Why both?

Why must signoff include both DRC and LVS?

Answer

They look at different things. DRC checks geometry: can it be built? LVS checks connectivity: is it the right circuit? Each is blind to what the other catches.

Exercise 8.3: Apply the rules

Using Table 8.2, say whether each shape is legal. (a) Two metal-1 wires, each 0.16 µm wide, 0.12 µm apart. (b) A metal-1 wire 0.12 µm wide and 5 µm long, far from anything else. (c) A metal-1 square 0.30 µm on a side.

Answer

(a) Illegal: the width is fine (0.16 ≥ 0.14) but the spacing, 0.12 µm, is below 0.14 µm (met1.2). (b) Illegal: the width 0.12 µm is below the 0.14 µm minimum (met1.1), even though its area, \(0.12 \times 5 = 0.6\) µm², is large enough. (c) Legal as far as these rules go: width 0.30 µm is above 0.14 µm, and the area \(0.30 \times 0.30 = 0.09\) µm² is above 0.083 µm².

Exercise 8.4: Break a design rule on purpose

In Magic with the Sky130 technology, you draw two metal-1 rectangles 0.10 µm apart and run drc check and drc why, then move them to 0.14 µm apart and check again. What do you expect to see? Explain in two sentences why a layout can be DRC clean and still fail LVS.

Answer

At 0.10 µm Magic reports a metal-1 spacing violation (rule met1.2, minimum 0.14 µm); at 0.14 µm the spacing is clean. DRC checks shapes only: two correctly spaced wires can still connect the wrong pins, and only LVS, which compares connectivity, can see that.

Exercise 8.5: Reading an LVS report

An LVS run prints "Circuit 1 contains 1842 devices, Circuit 2 contains 1840 devices." Can signoff proceed?

Answer

No. The device counts differ, so the layout and the source netlist cannot match. Two devices are missing from one side (an extra or deleted device, or one that was not recognised). The report names the unmatched devices and nets; they must be found and the mismatch resolved before signoff.

Exercise 8.6: Which check?

Match each problem to the check that finds it: (1) a net that is cut in two by a missing via; (2) a gate oxide ruptured by plasma charge; (3) a netlist that no longer matches the RTL after an ECO; (4) a dished, uneven metal layer.

Answer

(1) LVS (an open). (2) The antenna check. (3) Logic equivalence checking. (4) Density: metal fill added to bring every window into the density band.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Placement
docs.text:
The floorplan has fixed the die, the macros, the pins and the power grid, but the sea of standard cells is still floating with no physical home. Placement gives every cell an exact \((x, y)\) position in a row. It is a vast optimisation problem: hundreds of thousands or millions of cells, each with one legal place, and three goals that pull against one another. The cells must be close enough that wires are short, close enough on critical paths that timing is met, and yet spread out enough that the router can find room for every wire.

This chapter explains how placers measure wirelength before any wire exists, how they work in three phases from a smooth approximation to a legal and polished result, why congestion matters as much as length, and how the tool repairs timing against an ideal clock before the clock tree is built.

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you can:

  1. State the three objectives of placement and measure wirelength with HPWL.
  2. Describe global placement, legalisation and detailed placement, and say why they are separate.
  3. Explain congestion, and why the lowest wirelength is not always the best placement.
  4. Describe buffering, sizing and cloning, and say why setup is repaired before the clock tree and hold after it.

docs.title: 4.1 What placement is trying to do
docs.text:
After synthesis the design has hundreds of thousands of standard cells, and the floorplan is carved into rows of fixed height tiled with sites, the smallest legal step in the horizontal direction. Placement drops every cell onto a row and a site so that the design is routable, fast and uncongested. It balances three goals.

Short wires. Short nets mean less capacitance, less delay, less power and less to route. The universal proxy for length is HPWL, defined below.

Timing. Cells on a critical path should sit close together so that the nets joining them are short and fast. A placer that feeds timing information back into its choices is called timing-driven.

Avoiding crowding. If too many nets cross one region the router runs out of tracks. A congestion-driven placer spreads cells out so that local wiring demand stays below supply.

docs.title: 4.2 Measuring wirelength: HPWL
docs.text:
Real wires do not exist yet, so placers estimate them. Draw the smallest rectangle that encloses all the pins of a net, and take its width plus its height. That is the half-perimeter wirelength, HPWL:

\[\mathrm{HPWL}(\text{net}) = \bigl(\max_i x_i - \min_i x_i\bigr) + \bigl(\max_i y_i - \min_i y_i\bigr)\]

and the total over all nets is the quantity the placer minimises:
