\[\text{Total HPWL} = \sum_{\text{nets}} \mathrm{HPWL}(\text{net})\]

HPWL is cheap to compute, and for nets of two or three pins it equals the length of the shortest possible right-angled route. For nets with more pins it is a lower bound, but it remains the standard measure.

Example 4.1: HPWL of one net

A net connects pins at \((2, 1)\), \((7, 4)\) and \((3, 6)\).

  1. The \(x\) values run from 2 to 7, so the width is \(7 - 2 = 5\).
  2. The \(y\) values run from 1 to 6, so the height is \(6 - 1 = 5\).
  3. HPWL \(= 5 + 5 = 10\) (Figure 4.1).
Figure 4.1 Half-perimeter wirelength of a net. A three-pin net with the bounding box drawn around its pins; the width is 5 and the height is 5, so HPWL is 10.

Example 4.2: Being the placer

Six cells A to F sit on a grid of sites, joined by four nets: A–B–C, C–D, D–E–F and A–F. In the course's interactive placer the cells start scattered and the learner moves them to shrink the dashed boxes. Figure 4.2 shows the two extreme states.

Scattered: A\((0,0)\), B\((11,4)\), C\((6,0)\), D\((0,4)\), E\((11,0)\), F\((8,3)\). The nets measure A–B–C: \(11 + 4 = 15\); C–D: \(6 + 4 = 10\); D–E–F: \(11 + 4 = 15\); A–F: \(8 + 3 = 11\). The total is \(51\).

Well placed: A\((3,1)\), B\((3,2)\), C\((4,2)\), D\((5,2)\), E\((5,3)\), F\((4,1)\). The nets measure A–B–C: \(1 + 1 = 2\); C–D: \(1 + 0 = 1\); D–E–F: \(1 + 2 = 3\); A–F: \(1 + 0 = 1\). The total is \(7\).

The same cells and the same nets: moving them changes the wirelength by a factor of seven.

Figure 4.2 The same cells, scattered and well placed. Six cells on a grid with four nets drawn as dashed bounding boxes: scattered placement with total HPWL 51 on the left, and a compact placement with total HPWL 7 on the right.

docs.title: 4.3 Three phases: global, legalise, detailed
docs.text:
Modern placers split the work into three ordered phases, each tightening a constraint that the one before relaxed.

Global placement finds an approximate position for every cell, minimising total HPWL while spreading cells evenly. Cells may overlap and need not sit on legal sites; think of a smooth cloud of density. Analytic placers, such as OpenROAD's RePlAce, treat this as a non-linear optimisation, balancing a wirelength term against an electrostatic-style density penalty.

Legalisation removes every overlap and snaps each cell to a legal row and site, moving cells as little as possible so that the global solution is preserved. Cells may not straddle rows, overlap blockages or share a site. The course describes the legaliser in OpenROAD's dpl module as Abacus- or Tetris-style.

Detailed placement polishes the now-legal design locally: swapping neighbours, sliding cells along a row, mirroring them and filling gaps, to squeeze out the last of the wirelength and to fix small timing and pin-access problems, without creating overlaps again.

Think about it

Why not snap cells to sites from the very start?

Answer

Forcing cells onto discrete sites at every step turns a smooth, differentiable optimisation into a brutal combinatorial one. Global placement stays in continuous space so that mathematical optimisers can move millions of cells at once; discretisation is left to legalisation, where the moves are already small.

docs.title: 4.4 Short is not enough: congestion
docs.text:
A placement can have beautiful wirelength and still be impossible to route, because too many nets want to cross the same region. Placers therefore reason about the supply and demand of routing tracks.

  • Density maps. The core is diced into a grid of tiles, called g-cells (global-routing cells), and the placer tracks how full each bin is. A local density above the target, for instance over 100 % of the available sites, cannot be legalised and warns of coming congestion.
  • Congestion maps. A fast trial route estimates, for every tile edge, the routing demand divided by the number of tracks available. Hot spots, where demand exceeds supply (overflow above 1.0), are red flags long before the real wires are drawn.
  • Placement blockages keep channels open around macros, reserve space for buffers or steer cells away from congestion.
  • Target density. Deliberately leaving the core 60 to 70 % full gives the router and the clock-tree builder room to insert wires and buffers. Packing to 90 % or more is a classic recipe for failing to route.

Timing-driven placement feeds net weights or slack back from a timing engine, so that critical nets are pulled tighter, while congestion-driven placement inflates cells or spreads density in hot regions. The two aims fight, and a good placer balances them.

Common misconception

"The lowest wirelength is the best placement." Not necessarily. A placement that is optimal for wirelength often packs connected cells into a dense knot that the router cannot escape. Real placers accept a few per cent more wirelength for a much flatter congestion map: a slightly longer, routable design always beats a shorter, unroutable one.

docs.title: 4.5 Fixing timing before the clock is real
docs.text:
During placement the clock is assumed to be ideal: it reaches every flip-flop at the same instant with no delay. This is a fiction, since clock-tree synthesis builds the real network in the next chapter, but it is good enough to repair the data paths first, before the clock network muddies the picture. This pre-CTS optimisation (OpenROAD's resizer) repairs setup violations and design-rule problems with three moves.

Buffering. A long, heavily loaded or high-fan-out net is broken up with buffers that re-drive the signal. This cuts delay and fixes maximum-transition and maximum-capacitance violations.

Gate sizing. A weak cell is swapped for a stronger drive-strength variant, or the reverse, to trade speed against area and power until the slack target is met.

Cloning. A gate that drives too many loads is duplicated so that each copy drives a subset, splitting the fan-out and shortening the paths from the critical branch.

# OpenROAD: a typical pre-CTS (ideal-clock) resizing pass
estimate_parasitics -placement          ;# wire RC estimated from the placement
set_dont_use $dont_use_cells
buffer_ports
repair_design -max_wire_length 600      ;# buffers for long nets; fix slew and capacitance limits
repair_timing -setup                    ;# size gates and add buffers for setup
# hold is deliberately left until AFTER clock-tree synthesis

Think about it

Why fix setup now but leave hold for after the clock tree?

Answer

Setup depends on the data path being fast enough, which can be judged with an ideal clock. Hold depends on the real clock arrival at each flip-flop, and that arrival does not exist until the clock tree is built. Fixing hold against an ideal clock would waste buffers that would have to be redone.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Placement gives every cell an \((x, y)\) in the rows, balancing short wires (HPWL), timing and freedom from congestion.
  • HPWL is the width plus the height of the box around a net's pins; the total over all nets is the standard estimate of wirelength.
  • The phases are global (approximate, overlaps allowed), legalisation (snap to rows and sites) and detailed (local polish).
  • Density maps, trial-route congestion maps and blockages keep the design routable; wirelength alone is not the goal.
  • Before the clock tree, buffering, sizing and cloning fix setup against an ideal clock; hold waits until after it.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 4.1: HPWL of a net

A net connects pins at \((2, 1)\), \((7, 4)\) and \((3, 6)\). What is its HPWL? Now move the pin at \((7, 4)\) to \((4, 4)\). What is the HPWL?

Answer

\((7 - 2) + (6 - 1) = 10\). After the move the \(x\) values are 2, 4, 3, so the width is \(4 - 2 = 2\) and the height is still \(6 - 1 = 5\): HPWL \(= 7\).

Exercise 4.2: Two nets

Net N1 has pins at \((1, 1)\), \((4, 3)\) and \((2, 6)\); net N2 has pins at \((5, 5)\) and \((9, 2)\). Find the HPWL of each and the total.

Answer

N1: \((4 - 1) + (6 - 1) = 3 + 5 = 8\). N2: \((9 - 5) + (5 - 2) = 4 + 3 = 7\). Total \(= 15\).

Exercise 4.3: A different good placement

In the well-placed layout of Example 4.2, move F from \((4, 1)\) to \((5, 1)\), leaving the other cells where they are. Compute the new total HPWL and say whether placement can do better than 7 on this problem.

Answer

A–B–C is unchanged at 2 and C–D at 1. D–E–F has D\((5,2)\), E\((5,3)\), F\((5,1)\): width 0, height \(3 - 1 = 2\), so 2. A–F has A\((3,1)\) and F\((5,1)\): width 2, height 0, so 2. The total is \(2 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 7\), the same as before.

Can 7 be beaten? Three distinct sites need an HPWL of at least 2, and two distinct sites at least 1, so the four nets cannot total less than \(2 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 6\). That bound can be reached: put A\((0,0)\), B\((0,1)\), C\((0,2)\), D\((1,2)\), E\((1,1)\), F\((1,0)\). Then A–B–C \(= 2\), C–D \(= 1\), D–E–F \(= 2\), A–F \(= 1\), a total of 6. Since 6 is also the lower bound, it is the minimum. The course's placer treats 7 as the score to match, and 6 as the prize for a careful search.

Exercise 4.4: Knotted or spread?

A placement has the lowest total HPWL the tool has ever found, but the congestion map shows several tiles with overflow above 1.0. Is it a good placement? What would a placer do about it?

Answer

Not yet: routing will fail or take large detours in those tiles. The placer should spread cells in the hot regions, add blockages or lower the density target, accepting a little more wirelength for a flatter congestion map.

Exercise 4.5: Which repair first?

A net with fan-out of 40 is the start of the critical path. Name the three pre-CTS repairs and say which you would try first.

Answer

Buffering, gate sizing and cloning. Fan-out is the problem, so buffering the net (or cloning the driver so that each copy drives a share of the 40 loads) is the natural first move; up-sizing the driver also helps but makes the driver's own input heavier for the gate before it.

docs.title: About this book
docs.text:
A modern digital chip begins as a few thousand lines of Verilog and ends as a layout file, many gigabytes in size, from which a factory makes photographic masks. Everything between those two files is the subject of this book: logic synthesis, floorplanning, power planning, placement, clock-tree synthesis, routing, parasitic extraction, static timing analysis, physical verification and the final stream-out to GDSII. Together these steps are called the RTL-to-GDSII flow.

The book is a course text. It explains each stage in continuous prose, works the numbers by hand (slack, die size, wirelength, clock skew, wire delay), shows the real commands and configuration of the open-source flow, and then asks you to run that flow yourself on a small design. Nothing in it needs an industrial licence or a non-disclosure agreement. The tools are the free ones: Yosys for synthesis, OpenROAD for floorplanning, placement, clock-tree synthesis, routing and timing, Magic and KLayout for layout and design-rule checks, netgen for layout-versus-schematic checks, all driven by OpenLANE and targeting the SkyWater Sky130 open process kit.

In brief

Read the chapters in order. Each one opens with what it covers and why it matters, builds its ideas in numbered sections, shows worked examples in boxes, and closes with a summary and exercises whose answers are folded away until you open them.

docs.title: Who the book is for
docs.text: The book assumes that you know what a Verilog module is and have written a little synthesisable RTL: registers, an always block, an adder. It does not assume any knowledge of physical design. It suits a final-year undergraduate or a postgraduate course on VLSI design or digital design automation, and a self-taught reader who wants to understand what happens after the simulation passes. A reader who has met the companion books on hardware description languages and on microarchitecture will find the flow here a natural next step: those books describe the chip, this one makes it.

docs.title: How the chapters are arranged
docs.text:
Chapter Subject The question it answers 1 The RTL-to-GDSII flow What are the stages, files, goals and tools? 2 Logic synthesis and timing basics How do gates come out of RTL, and are they fast enough? 3 Floorplanning and power planning How big is the chip, and how does power reach every cell? 4 Placement Where does every cell sit? 5 Clock-tree synthesis Does the clock reach every flip-flop together? 6 Routing and parasitic extraction Can every net be drawn in metal, and what do the wires cost? 7 Static timing analysis With real wires, is every path fast enough and not too fast? 8 Physical verification and tapeout Can the factory build it, and is it the right circuit? 9 Running the flow with OpenLANE How do I do all of this myself, for free?

Timing ideas are introduced early, in Chapter 2, because synthesis is where timing first matters, and they are completed in Chapter 7 once clock skew and real wire delays can be included. The exercises that need a computer with the tools installed are collected at the end of Chapter 9 together with a capstone project; the paper exercises sit at the end of the chapter whose ideas they test.

docs.title: How to use the book
docs.text:
Work the paper problems before opening the answers. Slack, utilisation, wirelength and skew are all short calculations, and the habit of doing them by hand is what lets you read a tool's report with understanding. When you reach Chapter 9, keep a log of every command, configuration change and result; the tool exercises ask for tables built from each run's metrics file, a screenshot of the layout and a note of what changed between runs.

A word on numbers

Figures in worked examples are teaching values, chosen so that the arithmetic is easy to follow. Where a number comes from a real process, such as the Sky130 site size or a design-rule minimum, the text says so. Rule values given in the book are simplified for teaching and must never be used in place of the foundry's own rule manual.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text: Names of files, commands, configuration variables and cells are set in code font. Times are in nanoseconds (ns) or picoseconds (ps), lengths in micrometres (µm) and millimetres (mm), areas in µm². A figure or table is numbered by its chapter and its place in the chapter, as in Figure 3.1. Exercises are in boxes; each answer is in a folded box directly below it.

docs.title: Chapter 6: Routing and Parasitic Extraction
docs.text:
Placement has fixed where every cell sits and clock-tree synthesis has tamed the skew. Until now a connection such as "the output of this NAND feeds three flip-flops" has been only a line in the netlist. Routing lays down the actual copper: for every net it finds wire segments on the routing layers, joined by vias, that tie all the net's pins together without touching any other net and without breaking a single geometric rule of the process. A modern block has millions of nets and needs billions of individual shapes.

When the wires exist, they can be measured. Parasitic extraction records the resistance and capacitance of all that metal and writes it to a file, so that timing, until now an estimate, becomes real. This chapter covers the two passes of routing, the metal stack, the order in which things are routed, the design rules and two physical hazards (the antenna effect and crosstalk), and then extraction and the rule that explains why long wires are so slow.

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you can:

  1. Tell a net from a wire, and global routing from detailed routing.
  2. Describe the metal stack, vias, tracks, pitch and preferred directions.
  3. Explain the order power, clock, signals, and the main design rules a router obeys.
  4. Explain the antenna effect and crosstalk, and how routing avoids them.
  5. Explain parasitic extraction and SPEF, and use the rule that wire delay grows with the square of length.

docs.title: 6.1 From nets to metal
docs.text:
A net is a logical fact from the netlist: "these pins are connected". A wire (or interconnect) is the physical metal that makes it true: segments on several layers, joined by vias. One net becomes many wire segments. Routing turns every net into wires that connect all its pins, touch no other net and break no manufacturing rule.

A track is a legal centre line for a wire on a given layer, like a lane on a motorway. The pitch is the centre-to-centre distance between neighbouring tracks, typically the minimum width plus the minimum spacing. The set of all horizontal and vertical tracks forms the routing grid. If wires are kept on tracks, the spacing rules are satisfied automatically.

Solving the whole routing problem exactly in one step is computationally hopeless, so routing is done in two passes (like planning a road trip: first choose the motorways and the towns, then every turn and lane change).

Global routing Detailed routing Granularity coarse g-cells, each many tracks wide individual tracks and wire shapes Produces a plan: which tiles and layers each net uses, plus a congestion map real metal: wires, vias, layers Design rules ignored; only capacity counts all enforced: width, spacing, via and area Main question can everything fit, and where is it tight? draw legal, rule-clean wires Speed fast: minutes slow: the runtime bottleneck Output metric overflow and congestion DRC violations, wirelength, via count OpenROAD tool FastRoute (global_route) TritonRoute (detailed_route)

Table 6.1 The two passes of routing.

Global routing overlays a coarse grid of g-cells on the block. It assigns each net to a sequence of g-cells and to layers, treating the boundaries between g-cells as edges with limited capacity (the number of wires that can cross). If a region is over capacity the tool reports a congestion hot spot now, cheaply, before any real metal is committed; congestion is often the signal to loop back and change the placement or the floorplan.

Common misconception

"Global routing draws thin wires, and detailed routing thickens them." No. Global routing draws no metal at all: it only assigns nets to regions and layers and predicts congestion. Every wire and via in the final layout is created by detailed routing.

docs.title: 6.2 The metal stack
docs.text:
Interconnect is built as a vertical stack of metal layers separated by insulating dielectric and joined by vias (Figure 6.1). The layers are not alike.

  • Lower layers (met1, met2) are thin and dense: narrow, tightly pitched and of high resistance per unit length. They suit short local hops between nearby cells.
  • Upper layers are thick and wide: low resistance and a coarse pitch. They suit long signals, clock spines and the power grid. A long net routed on a thick upper layer has far less resistance, and therefore far less delay, than the same net squeezed onto met1.
  • Preferred directions alternate: one layer runs mostly horizontally, the next mostly vertically, and so on. A signal travels horizontally on one layer, rises through a via, continues vertically on the next, like a multi-storey road network.
  • A via is a small metal plug joining a wire on layer \(N\) to a wire on layer \(N+1\). Vias have their own rules (enclosure, a minimum count for wide wires) and add resistance and area, so routers avoid needless layer changes.
Figure 6.1 A metal stack: thin and dense below, thick and coarse above. A five-layer metal stack, met1 at the bottom to met5 at the top, getting thicker upwards, with arrows showing alternating preferred directions and green vias between layers, above the transistor layer and substrate.

The stack drawn is a simplified, Sky130-style five-metal stack. Process nodes with more layers extend the same pattern: the course's reference table lists, for a generic modern process, the top layers (M9 and M10) for the power grid, clock and long global routes, the intermediate layers for global signal routing and wide straps, mid layers for medium-length signals, M2 for short routing, M1 for cell-level connections and pins, then the poly and diffusion of the devices on the substrate.

docs.title: 6.3 Who is routed first
docs.text:
Not everything is routed at once, and not everything is routed the same way. Routing proceeds by priority.

  1. Power and ground are routed first, as special routing. The grid of wide straps and rings is usually built on the thick upper layers during floorplanning; it is in place before signals because signal routing has to weave round it. The standard-cell rails on met1 take their power from it.
  2. The clock comes next. The clock nets from CTS are routed early and carefully, often on higher, lower-resistance layers and with extra spacing or shielding, so that their delay and skew stay under tight control.
  3. Signals come last. The millions of ordinary data nets are routed into whatever tracks remain, honouring each layer's preferred direction.

The least flexible and most valuable networks go first; the flexible many fill in around them. Letting a million data nets take the best tracks first would force power and clock onto poor resources.

docs.title: 6.4 Design rules the router obeys
docs.text:
Every shape the detailed router draws must satisfy the foundry's design rules, the geometric constraints that guarantee the layout can be made.

Rule Why it exists Minimum width a thinner wire may not print, or may break (an open) Minimum spacing closer wires may print as one (a short), and couple strongly Via enclosure and via rules metal must overlap a via enough to connect reliably; legal via sizes, spacing and counts Minimum area tiny slivers of metal do not pattern well, so a shape sometimes needs a jog to add metal Density each region of each layer needs neither too little nor too much metal (fill is added later)

Table 6.2 Design rules that routing cares about most.

The router aims to be clean by construction, and the pitch is chosen so that on-track wires already meet the spacing rule. The authoritative check is the design-rule check (DRC) at signoff, treated in Chapter 8. Routing's job is to hand DRC as few violations as possible.

docs.title: 6.5 The antenna effect
docs.text:
The antenna effect is a manufacturing hazard, not a run-time one. Chips are built layer by layer, and each metal layer is etched with a plasma. While a given layer is being etched, a wire that is already connected to a transistor's thin gate oxide but not yet to any diffusion acts like an antenna: it collects charge from the plasma. If the connected metal area is large compared with the gate it feeds, the voltage can build up until it punches through the gate oxide, leaving a dead transistor discovered only after the wafer is finished.

Foundries therefore limit the antenna ratio: the area of metal connected to a gate must not exceed a given multiple of the gate area, on every layer at every fabrication step. Two cures are standard (Figure 6.2).

  • Layer jumping. Hop up to a higher layer and back down, breaking a long run. Because each layer is etched separately, less metal is exposed during any one etch.
  • Antenna diode. A small diode attached to the net near the gate gives the charge a safe path to the substrate.
Figure 6.2 The antenna effect and its two cures. Three panels: a long wire connected only to a thin gate collecting charge; a layer jump that breaks the run; a diode near the gate that bleeds the charge away.

The name has nothing to do with radio. A floating metal area harvests charge during fabrication and dumps it into a fragile gate.

docs.title: 6.6 Crosstalk
docs.text:
Two wires that run close and parallel form a small capacitor. When one, the aggressor, switches, it nudges the other, the victim. This is crosstalk, and its effects are two.

  • Glitch (noise). A bump of voltage on a quiet victim wire, which might be captured as a wrong value.
  • Delay change. If aggressor and victim switch together, the coupling can speed up or, worse, slow down the victim, pushing it out of its timing window.

Coupling capacitance grows with how long and how close two wires run in parallel, so routing controls it directly. The router's remedies are more spacing on sensitive nets, a grounded shield wire beside a critical net, shorter parallel runs and a different layer. Crosstalk cannot even be computed before routing, because the wires and their neighbours did not exist: that is why signal-integrity analysis waits for post-route parasitics.

docs.title: 6.7 Parasitic extraction: making timing real
docs.text:
A real wire is not an ideal connection. Metal has resistance \(R\) that grows with its length and shrinks with its cross-section, and capacitance \(C\) to the substrate and to neighbouring wires. Together they form a distributed RC network that delays and degrades every signal. These unwanted but unavoidable values are the wire's parasitics.

Parasitic extraction is the step that measures the \(R\) and \(C\) of every wire segment and via after routing and writes them out. Before routing, tools had only guesses: a wire-load model ("a net with three loads has roughly this much capacitance") or a rough estimate from the placement. That is why pre-route timing is only provisional. After extraction, timing uses the actual wires, and post-route analysis becomes the signoff-grade answer.

The results are written to a SPEF file (Standard Parasitic Exchange Format): a text file that lists, per net, the resistors and the capacitors (to ground and coupling to other nets) that model the routed interconnect. In OpenROAD, OpenRCX performs the extraction and writes the .spef, which the timing engine reads to annotate every net.

docs.title: Why long wires are so slow
docs.text:
Model a wire of length \(L\) as a distributed RC line. Both its resistance and its capacitance grow in proportion to its length, \(R = rL\) and \(C = cL\), where \(r\) and \(c\) are values per unit length. A first-order (Elmore) estimate of the delay of a distributed RC line is proportional to \(RC\):

\[\text{delay} \propto R \cdot C = (rL)(cL) = r\,c\,L^{2}.\]

Double the length and the delay roughly quadruples. This one rule explains three things at once.

  1. Long nets are routed on thick, low-resistance upper layers.
  2. Buffers chop a long wire into short pieces: several small \(L^2\) terms instead of one large one.
  3. Placement that shortens critical nets pays off enormously.

Example 6.1: Rescuing a long wire with buffers

Use the course's model: an unbuffered wire of length \(L\) mm has a delay of \(50\,L^2\) ps; each buffer adds 30 ps; \(n\) buffers cut the wire into \(n + 1\) equal pieces, each of length \(L/(n+1)\). The delay is

\[d(n) = (n+1)\cdot 50\left(\frac{L}{n+1}\right)^{2} + 30\,n = \frac{50\,L^{2}}{n+1} + 30\,n .\]

Unbuffered wires. A 2 mm wire takes \(50 \times 4 = 200\) ps; a 4 mm wire \(50 \times 16 = 800\) ps; a 6 mm wire \(50 \times 36 = 1800\) ps. Twice the length, four times the delay.

A 4 mm wire with \(n = 0\) to \(6\) buffers. With \(50\,L^2 = 800\):

Buffers \(n\) \(800/(n+1)\) \(+ 30\,n\) Delay (ps) 0 800 0 800 1 400 30 430 2 266.7 60 326.7 3 200 90 290 4 160 120 280 5 133.3 150 283.3 6 114.3 180 294.3

The best is \(n = 4\) at 280 ps (Figure 6.3). Beyond that, each extra buffer saves less wire delay, because the \(L^2\) terms are already small, while still costing its fixed 30 ps.

Figure 6.3 Wire delay grows as L squared; buffers have an optimum. Left: delay against length for an unbuffered wire, rising as a parabola to 1800 ps at 6 mm. Right: bars for the delay of a 4 mm wire with 0 to 6 buffers, lowest at 4 buffers (280 ps).

docs.title: 6.8 The real commands
docs.text:
In the OpenROAD and OpenLANE flow, global routing is done by FastRoute, detailed routing by TritonRoute (the drt router) and extraction by OpenRCX. A representative Tcl sequence follows.

# --- Global routing (FastRoute): plan regions, report congestion ---
set_routing_layers -signal met1-met5 -clock met3-met5
set_global_routing_layer_adjustment met1-met5 0.5
global_route -guide_file route.guide -congestion_iterations 30 -verbose

# --- Detailed routing (TritonRoute): real wires and vias, rule-clean ---
detailed_route -output_drc route_drc.rpt -output_maze maze.log \
               -bottom_routing_layer met1 -top_routing_layer met5 -verbose 1

# --- Antenna check and repair ---
check_antennas
repair_antennas                       ;# inserts diodes or requests layer jumps

# --- Parasitic extraction (OpenRCX) -> SPEF ---
define_process_corner -ext_model_index 0 X
extract_parasitics -ext_model_file rcx_patterns.rules
write_spef routed.spef                ;# the file timing and signoff will read

# --- Post-route timing now uses real parasitics ---
read_spef routed.spef
report_checks -path_delay max         ;# signoff-grade STA (Chapter 7)

The resulting routed.spef is the file that Chapter 7 feeds to static timing analysis, and the routed layout is what Chapter 8 runs DRC and LVS on.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Routing turns nets into wires. Global routing (FastRoute) plans g-cells and layers and predicts congestion; detailed routing (TritonRoute) draws real, rule-clean wires and vias on legal tracks.
  • The metal stack has thin, dense lower layers for local hops and thick, coarse upper layers for long nets, clock and power, joined by vias, with alternating preferred directions.
  • Routing order is power, then clock, then signals. The antenna effect is cured by layer jumps or diodes; crosstalk by spacing, shields and shorter parallel runs.
  • Extraction measures every wire's \(R\) and \(C\) into a SPEF file. Wire delay grows as \(L^2\), which is why buffers and good placement matter.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 6.1: Scaling a wire

A 2 mm wire has 200 ps of RC delay. Roughly how much does an unbuffered 6 mm wire have?

Answer

Three times the length gives about \(3^2 = 9\) times the delay: roughly 1800 ps.

Exercise 6.2: Why clock first?

Why is the clock routed before ordinary signals?

Answer

Its skew must stay tightly controlled, so it needs the best layers and the extra spacing before millions of signal nets take them.

Exercise 6.3: The buffer table

Using \(d(n) = 50\,L^2/(n+1) + 30\,n\), compute the delay of a 2 mm wire with 0, 1, 2 and 3 buffers. Which is best?

Answer

With \(50\,L^2 = 200\): \(n = 0\): 200 ps. \(n = 1\): \(100 + 30 = 130\) ps. \(n = 2\): \(66.7 + 60 = 126.7\) ps. \(n = 3\): \(50 + 90 = 140\) ps. Two buffers is best (126.7 ps).

Exercise 6.4: The optimum number of buffers

Treating \(n\) as a continuous variable, find the \(n\) that minimises \(d(n)\), and compare with Example 6.1 for \(L = 4\). For \(L = 6\), find the best whole number of buffers.

Answer

Set \(d'(n) = -50\,L^2/(n+1)^2 + 30 = 0\), so \(n + 1 = L\sqrt{50/30} \approx 1.29\,L\). For \(L = 4\) this gives \(n + 1 \approx 5.16\), so \(n \approx 4.2\), consistent with the best whole number \(n = 4\). For \(L = 6\), \(n + 1 \approx 7.75\); comparing whole numbers: \(d(6) = 1800/7 + 180 = 437.1\) ps, \(d(7) = 1800/8 + 210 = 435\) ps, \(d(8) = 1800/9 + 240 = 440\) ps. The best is \(n = 7\) at 435 ps, down from 1800 ps unbuffered.

Exercise 6.5: Global or detailed?

For each statement, say whether it describes global or detailed routing: (a) it reports a congestion map; (b) it snaps wires to tracks and drops vias; (c) it ignores spacing rules; (d) it is the slow part of the flow.

Answer

(a) Global. (b) Detailed. (c) Global: only capacity counts. (d) Detailed.

Exercise 6.6: Antenna or crosstalk?

A long met2 wire is connected only to one transistor gate and the foundry reports an antenna violation. Name the two cures. A different quiet wire shows a voltage bump whenever its neighbour switches. What is this and what are two cures?

Answer

Antenna cures: layer jumping (route part of the run up to a higher layer and back down) or inserting an antenna diode near the gate. The bump is crosstalk noise (a glitch) from an aggressor neighbour; cures include more spacing, a grounded shield wire alongside, a shorter parallel run or moving one of the nets to another layer.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Running the Flow with OpenLANE
docs.text:
Everything in the earlier chapters, synthesis, floorplan, placement, clock tree, routing, timing, DRC and LVS, and tapeout, is real software that you can run for free on your own machine. This chapter is a practical, step-by-step laboratory. You install the open-source toolchain, configure a small design, push it from RTL to a GDSII file with one command, inspect what came out, and then deliberately break timing and change utilisation to see how the tools react. At the end, a set of exercises and a capstone project asks you to repeat the process on designs of your own.

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you can:

  1. Name the tools of the open-source stack and the stage each one owns.
  2. Install OpenLANE with the Sky130 PDK and configure a design.
  3. Run RTL to GDSII with one command and find the outputs.
  4. Read WNS and TNS, DRC and LVS results and the area and utilisation of a run.
  5. Run experiments (a tighter clock, a higher utilisation) and explain the results.

docs.title: 9.1 The open-source stack
docs.text:
There is no single "chip compiler". The flow is a pipeline of specialist tools, each owning one stage, stitched together by an orchestrator (Figure 9.1).

Figure 9.1 The open-source stack. OpenLANE at the top driving Yosys with abc, OpenROAD (with RePlAce, TritonCTS, FastRoute, TritonRoute, OpenRCX and OpenSTA inside it), Magic, KLayout and netgen, all resting on the Sky130A PDK. Tool What it owns What it produces OpenLANE orchestration runs every step in order, applies the configuration, collects reports and tags runs Yosys (with abc) logic synthesis a gate-level netlist .v mapped to Sky130 cells OpenROAD floorplan, placement, clock tree, routing, timing DEF files, the routed database, timing reports OpenSTA, TritonCTS, FastRoute, TritonRoute static timing, clock tree, global and detailed routing (inside OpenROAD) slack reports, a balanced clock, a routed design Magic layout, DRC, GDS stream-out, extraction DRC report, .gds, parasitics KLayout viewing and a second DRC opinion views and checks of the final GDS netgen LVS the layout-versus-netlist report Sky130A PDK the target process .lib, .lef, rules, standard-cell layouts

Table 9.1 Who does what.

OpenLANE is the conductor. It is a set of Tcl scripts and a configuration system that calls each underlying tool in the right order, hands the output of one stage to the next and collects the reports. It does not do synthesis or routing itself. OpenLANE was created by Efabless around the SkyWater Sky130 PDK to support the free shuttle programme for open-source chips.

Think of a software compiler toolchain. Yosys is the front end, which lowers source to an intermediate form; OpenROAD is the back end and optimiser (instruction selection and scheduling, here placement, routing, clock tree and timing); OpenLANE is the make that runs the passes in order; and the Sky130 PDK is the target machine you compile for. The PDK ships the standard-cell libraries (sky130_fd_sc_hd, the high-density family, is the common default), the timing .lib files, the physical .lef abstracts, the layer and DRC rules and the cell layouts, everything the tools need to know about the process.

docs.title: 9.2 Installing the toolchain
docs.text:
You have three realistic routes; pick one.

Option A: Docker-based OpenLANE (the classic OpenLANE 1, recommended). The tools are notoriously fiddly to build, so OpenLANE ships them in a Docker image and you need only Docker, Python and make. This is the most reproducible route and matches almost every tutorial.

# Needs git, docker, make, python3 (on Windows, work inside WSL2)
git clone https://github.com/The-OpenROAD-Project/OpenLane.git
cd OpenLane

# Pull the tool image and install the Sky130 PDK (through ciel, formerly volare)
make

# To manage the PDK explicitly:
pip install ciel                 # formerly 'volare'
ciel enable --pdk sky130

# Smoke test: run the bundled SPM example design end to end
make test
# -> prints "Basic test passed" and creates a runs/ folder when all is well

The PDK is large and versioned. ciel (recently renamed from volare) is a small package manager that fetches a pre-built, known-good Sky130 build and pins its version, so that your results can be reproduced; make calls it for you and you rarely run it by hand.

Option B: OpenLane 2 with Nix. OpenLane was re-architected in Python, away from the Tcl-heavy version 1. It is installed with Nix, which pins exact tool versions declaratively, or as a Python package, and exposes the flow as composable Python steps. The ideas of this chapter carry over; the entry commands differ.

# OpenLane 2 (nix-shell gives a shell with every tool at a pinned version)
git clone https://github.com/efabless/openlane2.git
cd openlane2
nix-shell
openlane --dockerized ./designs/spm/config.json

Option C: the cloud. If you cannot install locally, run the Docker image on any Linux virtual machine, in a GitHub Codespace, or in a notebook environment that installs the flow with pip. This needs no set-up and suits a first look.

Common misconception

"OpenLANE is the tool that does synthesis and routing." It is not: OpenLANE is only the driver. When a run fails in, say, detailed routing, the real error and its log come from TritonRoute inside OpenROAD, not from OpenLANE. Always read the failing stage's own log in runs/<tag>/logs/, and not just OpenLANE's top-level output.

docs.title: 9.3 A design folder and its configuration
docs.text:
Every design lives in its own folder under designs/. The minimum is the Verilog sources and a configuration file.

OpenLane/
  designs/
    my_counter/
      src/
        counter.v          # your RTL (one or more .v files)
      config.json          # the design's configuration (config.tcl is the legacy form)

The configuration says what to build and sets the key knobs. JSON is the modern format; Tcl is the legacy equivalent. A realistic minimal config.json:

{
  "DESIGN_NAME":   "counter",
  "VERILOG_FILES": "dir::src/counter.v",
  "CLOCK_PORT":    "clk",
  "CLOCK_PERIOD":  10.0,

  "FP_CORE_UTIL":      45,
  "PL_TARGET_DENSITY": 0.55
}
Key Meaning Typical value DESIGN_NAME the top module's name; it must equal the name in the Verilog "counter" VERILOG_FILES the RTL sources; dir:: is relative to the design folder "dir::src/*.v" CLOCK_PORT the name of the clock input in the RTL "clk" CLOCK_PERIOD the target clock period in ns; it drives every timing check 10.0 (100 MHz) FP_CORE_UTIL the target core utilisation, %, for the initial floorplan 40 to 50 PL_TARGET_DENSITY the placement density target (0 to 1), usually a little above utilisation divided by 100 0.5 to 0.6 DIE_AREA, FP_SIZING a fixed die box "x0 y0 x1 y1" when FP_SIZING is "absolute"; otherwise the die is sized from the utilisation "0 0 150 150"

Table 9.2 The essential configuration keys.

You control the size of the die in one of two ways: give an absolute DIE_AREA, or let OpenLANE size the die from FP_CORE_UTIL, so that it fits your cells at that utilisation. Use utilisation-based sizing while you iterate, and pin an absolute size only when you must meet a fixed footprint. The two are alternatives: with FP_SIZING set to "absolute" the die is fixed by DIE_AREA, so a configuration that sets both an absolute size and a utilisation, as the course's sample page does, makes the utilisation setting meaningless. The configuration above uses relative sizing only. The area and utilisation arithmetic is that of Chapter 3.

docs.title: 9.4 Lab 1: a design from RTL to GDSII
docs.text:
Push a real design through. Here is a small synchronous counter, saved as designs/my_counter/src/counter.v.

module counter #(parameter WIDTH = 8) (
    input  wire              clk,
    input  wire              rst_n,
    input  wire              en,
    output reg  [WIDTH-1:0]  count
);
    always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
        if (!rst_n)      count <= {WIDTH{1'b0}};
        else if (en)     count <= count + 1'b1;
    end
endmodule

(For a meatier design, replace it with a small ALU, such as the add, subtract, and, or, xor, set-less-than and shift unit built in the HDL book, and set DESIGN_NAME and CLOCK_PORT to match.) Now run the whole flow with one command.

# From the OpenLane repository root
make mount                                  # enter the tool container
./flow.tcl -design my_counter -tag run1     # the WHOLE flow, with a run name of your own

# Handy variants:
./flow.tcl -design my_counter                                 # tagged automatically by date
./flow.tcl -design my_counter -from synthesis -to routing     # part of the flow
./flow.tcl -design my_counter -interactive                    # step through it (Section 9.7)

OpenLANE marches through the stages, the same pipeline as the rest of this book.

# Stage Tool What happens 1 synthesis Yosys with abc RTL becomes a netlist of sky130_fd_sc_hd cells; first area and cell-count report 2 floorplan and power grid OpenROAD die and core, rows, I/O pins, power ring and straps 3 placement OpenROAD (RePlAce) global, then detailed placement and legalisation 4 clock tree TritonCTS clock buffers inserted to balance skew 5 routing FastRoute, then TritonRoute global, then detailed routing on the metal stack 6 extraction, timing, DRC, LVS, GDS OpenRCX, OpenSTA, Magic, netgen parasitics (SPEF), static timing, DRC, LVS, antenna check, GDS stream-out

Table 9.3 The stages of an OpenLANE run.

Every run has its own folder, and the output tree is where you will spend your time.

designs/my_counter/runs/run1/
  results/
    synthesis/     counter.v                 # the gate-level netlist
    floorplan/     counter.def
    placement/     counter.def
    cts/           counter.def
    routing/       counter.def               # fully routed
    final/
      gds/         counter.gds               # the final GDSII: the tapeout file
      def/  lef/  spef/  verilog/            # final views for reuse
  reports/         area, timing, DRC and LVS summaries per stage
                   metrics.csv               # the headline numbers, one line
  logs/            each tool's own log: read these when something fails
  config.tcl, cmds.log                       # exactly what was run

Milestone

When the run finishes green, runs/run1/results/final/gds/counter.gds is a real, DRC-clean physical layout of your design in 130 nm silicon. That one file is what a foundry would turn into masks. You have run a tapeout-quality flow on your own computer.

docs.title: 9.5 Lab 2: reading the results
docs.text:
A green run is not the end; the reports say how good the result is. Four things to check.

a) Look at it. Open the layout in KLayout (fast and cross-platform) or in Magic with the Sky130 technology.

klayout designs/my_counter/runs/run1/results/final/gds/counter.gds

magic -T sky130A.tech designs/my_counter/runs/run1/results/final/gds/counter.gds

You will see rows of cells, power rails at the top and bottom of each row, coloured metal above them and vias stitching the layers. Zoom in far enough and the individual gates appear.

b) Timing. Read the worst and total negative slack.

cat designs/my_counter/runs/run1/reports/signoff/*sta*summary*.rpt

# in OpenSTA or interactive OpenROAD:
report_checks -path_delay max -fields {slew cap input nets fanout} -format full_clock
report_wns
report_tns

WNS \(\ge 0\) means that every path meets timing at your CLOCK_PERIOD. A negative WNS is the single worst path's shortfall in ns, and TNS sums all violations, telling you how widespread the problem is (Chapter 7).

c) Physical checks. Signoff must be clean to tape out.

cat designs/my_counter/runs/run1/reports/signoff/*drc*.rpt     # want: 0 violations
cat designs/my_counter/runs/run1/reports/signoff/*lvs*.rpt     # want: "Circuits match uniquely."

d) Area and utilisation.

grep -i "area\|cell count" designs/my_counter/runs/run1/reports/synthesis/*stat*.rpt
grep -i "util\|die\|core_area" designs/my_counter/runs/run1/reports/metrics.csv

A modern OpenLANE run also writes a single metrics.csv that collects the headline numbers (area, utilisation, WNS, TNS, DRC count, wirelength, power): the fastest way to compare runs at a glance.

docs.title: 9.6 Experiments
docs.text: Now make the tools react. Change one knob, run again, compare metrics.csv.

docs.title: Experiment 1: break timing on purpose
docs.text:
Tighten the clock aggressively.

# in config.json: "CLOCK_PERIOD": 2.0      (was 10.0: 100 MHz becomes 500 MHz)
./flow.tcl -design my_counter -tag fast_clk

Predict first: will setup or hold fail? Setup, because the clock period appears only in the setup check. Expect WNS to go negative and TNS to grow; the run may still complete, but it flags the timing violations. The critical path in the report is the carry chain of count + 1. Raise the period step by step, 3.0, 4.0 and so on, until WNS \(\ge 0\) again. That period is your design's \(f_{max}\), timing closure in miniature.

docs.title: Experiment 2: pack it tighter
docs.text:
# in config.json: "FP_CORE_UTIL": 65 (was 45), "PL_TARGET_DENSITY": 0.72 (raised to match)
./flow.tcl -design my_counter -tag dense

The die shrinks, which is cheaper. But congestion rises, routing takes longer, and if you push far enough routing fails or DRC errors appear. Compare die area, wirelength and WNS between run1 and dense. That triangle of area, timing and routability is what physical designers live in. High utilisation gives a small, cheap die that is congested and hard to route; low utilisation is easy to route and better for timing but costlier. There is no universally right number: the flow is a search.

docs.title: 9.7 Driving the flow step by step
docs.text:
Sometimes you want to drive the physical stages by hand, to debug, to try a command or to understand what OpenLANE automates. There are two ways in. First, OpenLANE's interactive mode runs the flow one step at a time from a Tcl prompt.

./flow.tcl -design my_counter -interactive
# then, at the interactive prompt:
package require openlane
prep -design my_counter
run_synthesis
run_floorplan
run_placement
run_cts
run_routing
run_magic            ;# DRC and GDS
run_lvs
# inspect the results after any step before going on

Second, OpenROAD has its own Tcl shell, so you can read the physical views and run individual engines directly.

openroad
# --- load the design ---
read_lef     merged.lef
read_def     results/floorplan/counter.def
read_liberty sky130_fd_sc_hd__tt_025C_1v80.lib

# --- run engines by hand ---
global_placement -density 0.55
detailed_placement
clock_tree_synthesis -buf_list sky130_fd_sc_hd__clkbuf_4
global_route
detailed_route

# --- analyse ---
report_checks -path_delay max        ;# setup
report_checks -path_delay min        ;# hold
report_wns ; report_tns
write_def  out.def
write_verilog out.v

Interactive mode is how you learn what each OpenLANE variable really does and how you debug one failing stage: reproduce just that step, change a command and rerun it in seconds instead of rerunning the whole flow. Every command above is what OpenLANE issues under the hood.

docs.title: 9.8 When things go wrong
docs.text:
Symptom Likely cause and fix routing fails, "unroutable" utilisation or density too high: lower FP_CORE_UTIL and PL_TARGET_DENSITY, or enlarge the die negative WNS the clock is too ambitious: loosen CLOCK_PERIOD, or let synthesis work harder (SYNTH_STRATEGY); check that the clock port name is right empty netlist, "no such module" DESIGN_NAME is not the top module, or a file is missing from VERILOG_FILES DRC errors at signoff often over-dense placement or the power grid: reduce density and read the rule name in the report "PDK not found" rerun make or ciel enable; check that PDK_ROOT points at your Sky130 installation the real error is not in OpenLANE's top log open the failing tool's file in runs/<tag>/logs/<stage>/ Docker permission denied add your user to the docker group (Linux) and log in again; on Windows use WSL2
