docs.title: 9.9 Where to go next
docs.text: The OpenLANE documentation (openlane.readthedocs.io, with the sources at github.com/The-OpenROAD-Project/OpenLane and github.com/efabless/openlane2) lists every configuration variable and many example designs. OpenROAD's documentation (openroad.readthedocs.io, theopenroadproject.org) is the command reference for the place-and-route and timing engine. The SkyWater process is documented at skywater-pdk.readthedocs.io and github.com/google/skywater-pdk. Matt Venn's "Zero to ASIC" course (zerotoasiccourse.com) and Tiny Tapeout (tinytapeout.com) are the fastest way from here to a fabricated chip.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• OpenLANE orchestrates Yosys, OpenROAD, Magic, KLayout and netgen for the Sky130 PDK; it does not do the work itself.
  • One folder per design: Verilog plus config.json (name, files, clock port and period, utilisation).
  • ./flow.tcl -design <name> runs RTL to GDSII; results are in runs/<tag>/, and the GDS is in results/final/gds/.
  • Check WNS and TNS, DRC equal to zero, an LVS match, and area and utilisation in metrics.csv. Then experiment: tighten the clock, raise the utilisation, and feel the trade-offs.
  • When a stage fails, read that tool's own log, and reproduce the failure in interactive mode.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
The paper exercises of this book are at the ends of the earlier chapters. These need the tools. Keep a log of every command, configuration change and result, and name every OpenLANE run with -tag. Every report should include the tool versions and the PDK version, the config.json used, a table built from each run's metrics.csv, a screenshot of the layout in KLayout, and what changed between runs and why.

Exercise 9.1: Synthesise a counter with Yosys

Use the counter of Section 9.4. Run Yosys for WIDTH = 8, 16 and 32 and record the cell counts by type:

yosys -p "read_verilog counter.v;
          chparam -set WIDTH 16 counter;
          synth -top counter; stat"

Then map to Sky130: after synth, run dfflibmap -liberty $LIB, abc -liberty $LIB and stat -liberty $LIB (LIB is the typical sky130_fd_sc_hd Liberty file) and record the area. Plot cells and area against WIDTH.

Answer

The flip-flop count equals WIDTH exactly (8, 16, 32): one per bit of count. The logic for + 1 and the enable grows roughly in proportion, so total cells and area grow about linearly with WIDTH. Open the netlist: no + remains, only library cells.

Exercise 9.2: Your first RTL-to-GDSII run

Install OpenLANE and pass make test. Create designs/my_counter with the 8-bit counter and the configuration of Section 9.3, and run it with -tag base. From the reports record the cell count, die area, utilisation, WNS, TNS, DRC count, LVS result and total wirelength. Open the GDS in KLayout and find a flip-flop, a power rail and a via; take a screenshot of each.

Answer

At a 10 ns clock an 8-bit counter meets timing easily: WNS \(\ge 0\) and TNS \(= 0\). Signoff must show 0 DRC errors and "Circuits match uniquely". The cell count includes many cells you did not write: fill, tap, decap and buffer cells inserted by the flow.

Exercise 9.3: Timing closure, find f_max

Set WIDTH to 32. Run at CLOCK_PERIOD = 10, 5, 3 and 2 ns (one tag each) and record WNS and TNS. Narrow down by binary search to the shortest period with WNS \(\ge 0\). Open the critical-path report at a failing period and say which cells are on it. Plot WNS against the period.

Answer

WNS falls as the period shrinks and crosses zero at your \(f_{max}\). TNS is 0 until then and then grows quickly as many bits fail together. The critical path runs through the carry chain of count + 1, from the low bits to the top bit: the longer the counter, the longer the chain.

Exercise 9.4: A utilisation sweep

Use the 32-bit counter, or a small ALU, at a comfortable clock. Run with FP_CORE_UTIL = 30, 45, 60 and 75 (raising PL_TARGET_DENSITY to roughly utilisation divided by 100 plus 0.1). Tabulate die area, wirelength, WNS, run time and DRC count. Push further until a run fails: which stage failed, and what did its log say?

Answer

Die area falls as utilisation rises; wirelength usually falls a little too, because cells are closer together. Beyond some point congestion rises, routing run time grows, and eventually placement or routing fails, or DRC errors appear. The failing stage's log, under runs/<tag>/logs/, names the problem.

Exercise 9.5: Where to look, and what changes

(a) Your run fails in detailed routing. Where do you look first? (b) You raise FP_CORE_UTIL from 45 to 65. Name one thing that improves and two that may get worse.

Answer

(a) In the detailed router's own log in runs/<tag>/logs/, not in OpenLANE's summary. (b) Better: smaller die area. Worse: congestion and routability, and timing (less room for buffers); possibly DRC errors as well.

Exercise 9.6: Capstone: your own design to GDSII

Choose something small and testable: a PWM generator, a stopwatch, the UART transmitter from the HDL book, a tiny ALU. Verify it first with a self-checking testbench. Write down the clock you aim for and why (the SDC-level goals). Run OpenLANE and iterate until WNS \(\ge 0\) at your target, DRC \(= 0\) and LVS matches. Write up the design, the testbench results, the final metrics, the layout and the two hardest problems you solved.

Answer

There is no single answer; a suggested marking guide is verified RTL 25 %, clean signoff (timing, DRC, LVS) 35 %, experiments and iteration log 20 %, report and reflection 20 %. For going further, Tiny Tapeout (tinytapeout.com) can put a design like this on a real shared chip, and for a modest fee your GDS comes back as a physical chip you can hold.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Static Timing Analysis
docs.text:
Placement, clock-tree synthesis and routing have committed the design to real cells, a real clock network and real parasitics. Now comes the question that decides whether the chip works at speed: does every path meet timing? Static timing analysis (STA) answers it exhaustively, for millions of paths, at every operating condition, without applying a single test vector. It is the gatekeeper of tapeout.

Chapter 2 introduced setup and hold slack for an ideal clock. This chapter completes them with clock skew and uncertainty, shows how to read the summary numbers (WNS and TNS) and a real timing report line by line, explains why a chip must be analysed at several corners, and sets out the opposite remedies for setup and hold violations.

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you can:

  1. Explain what makes timing analysis static, and list the four kinds of timing path.
  2. Compute setup and hold slack including skew and uncertainty, and explain why hold ignores the clock period.
  3. Interpret WNS and TNS, and read a timing report line by line.
  4. Explain PVT corners, multi-corner multi-mode analysis, on-chip variation and temperature inversion.
  5. Choose the right remedy for a setup or a hold violation.

docs.title: 7.1 What STA is
docs.text:
Static timing analysis adds up the propagation delay along every path of the gate-level design and compares it with the time the clock allows. "Static" means that no input stimulus is applied: STA needs no testbench, no vectors and no idea of what the logic does. It walks the delay graph once and checks every path, a coverage that no amount of dynamic simulation could match. Where a simulation exercises the few scenarios you thought to write, STA proves a bound that holds for all inputs.

The price of this generality is that STA is topological. It will happily report paths that can never occur in practice (false paths) and paths whose launch and capture are more than one cycle apart (multicycle paths). You tell the tool about them with SDC constraints, so that it does not flag phantom violations.

STA rests on three pieces of data from earlier stages: cell delays from the .lib, wire resistance and capacitance from the .spef, and the clock definition and exceptions from the .sdc.

A timing path runs from a startpoint (the clock pin of a register, or a primary input) to an endpoint (the data pin of a register, or a primary output). STA checks every startpoint-to-endpoint path against both a maximum-delay constraint (setup) and a minimum-delay constraint (hold). There are four families of path.

Path From To Bounded by register to register launch flip-flop's clock pin capture flip-flop's data pin the clock period: the usual critical paths input to register primary input capture flip-flop's data pin set_input_delay register to output launch flip-flop's clock pin primary output set_output_delay input to output primary input primary output pure logic straight through

Table 7.1 The four kinds of timing path.

STA turns a hard question, "will this chip ever fail at speed, for any input?", into an arithmetic one it can answer for every path at once: compare when data arrives at an endpoint with when it is required there. The difference is the slack.

docs.title: 7.2 The full setup check
docs.text:
The setup rule is the basic synchronous rule: data launched by one clock edge must be stable at the capture flip-flop before the next capture edge, less the flip-flop's setup time. Let the launch flip-flop's clock arrive at \(t_{launch}\) and the capture flip-flop's at \(t_{capture}\). Then

\[t_{arrival} = t_{launch} + t_{cq} + t_{logic,max}\] \[t_{required} = t_{capture} + T - t_{su} - t_{unc}\] \[\text{setup slack} = t_{required} - t_{arrival} \;\ge\; 0.\]

Here \(t_{unc}\) is the clock uncertainty, a margin for jitter (the clock edge wobbling from cycle to cycle) plus safety; it always eats slack. Writing skew \(= t_{capture} - t_{launch}\) and taking the launch edge as time zero, this collapses to the form used in the rest of the book:

\[\text{setup slack} = (T + \text{skew} - t_{su} - t_{unc}) - (t_{cq} + t_{logic,max}).\]

Example 7.1: Full setup check

\(T = 5.0\) ns, \(t_{cq} = 0.40\), slowest logic \(3.20\), \(t_{su} = 0.30\), \(t_{unc} = 0.10\), skew \(= 0.10\) ns.

  1. Arrival \(= 0.40 + 3.20 = 3.60\) ns.
  2. Required \(= 5.0 + 0.10 - 0.30 - 0.10 = 4.70\) ns.
  3. Slack \(= 4.70 - 3.60 = +1.10\) ns: met.

At \(T = 3.5\) ns:

  1. Required \(= 3.5 + 0.10 - 0.30 - 0.10 = 3.20\) ns.
  2. Slack \(= 3.20 - 3.60 = -0.40\) ns: violated. The clock has outrun the logic.

(Here skew and uncertainty happen to cancel, so the numbers equal those of Example 2.1.)

docs.title: 7.3 The full hold check
docs.text:
Hold is the mirror image, and the more treacherous half. The data launched by an edge must not race through so fast that it corrupts the value that the same edge is capturing at the downstream flip-flop, which needs its current data to stay stable for \(t_h\) after the edge. The minimum logic delay is used, because the fastest way through is the dangerous one:

\[\text{hold slack} = (t_{cq} + t_{logic,min}) - (t_h + \text{skew} + t_{unc}) \;\ge\; 0.\]

The period \(T\) does not appear. Both effects in a hold check come from the same clock edge: the check compares two consequences of one clock event at the two flip-flops. Slowing the clock does nothing for hold (Figure 7.1).

Example 7.2: Full hold check

\(t_{cq} = 0.40\), fastest logic \(0.30\), \(t_h = 0.15\), skew \(= 0.10\), \(t_{unc} = 0.10\) ns.

  1. Earliest arrival of new data \(= 0.40 + 0.30 = 0.70\) ns.
  2. Deadline \(= 0.15 + 0.10 + 0.10 = 0.35\) ns.
  3. Slack \(= 0.70 - 0.35 = +0.35\) ns: met.

Now let the skew grow to \(0.60\) ns (the capture clock arrives much later than the launch clock):

  1. Deadline \(= 0.15 + 0.60 + 0.10 = 0.85\) ns.
  2. Slack \(= 0.70 - 0.85 = -0.15\) ns: violated. The skew that helped setup has broken hold.
Figure 7.1 The hold check on a time line. A time line of the hold check: the capture edge at +0.10 ns, the hold time and uncertainty running to 0.35 ns, and new data arriving at 0.70 ns after clock-to-Q of 0.40 and fastest logic of 0.30; the slack is 0.35 ns.

Why hold is the dangerous one

A setup failure means the chip will not run at full speed; slow the clock and it works, so a setup problem can often be worked round in the laboratory. A hold failure is not frequency dependent: the part is broken at every clock speed, even the slowest. There is no knob on the tester that fixes it. If a hold violation escapes to silicon the chip is useless and the masks must be remade. That is why hold is closed conservatively, at the fast corner.

docs.title: 7.4 The clock's imperfections
docs.text:
An ideal clock reaches every flip-flop at once. A real clock, distributed by a buffer tree across millimetres of die, does not.

Effect What it is Effect on timing Latency delay from the clock source to a flip-flop's clock pin, split into source latency and network latency cancels in a register-to-register check if equal at both ends; only the difference matters Skew the difference in arrival between two related flip-flops, capture minus launch helps one check and hurts the other: setup gains when capture is later, hold loses Jitter and uncertainty cycle-to-cycle variation of the edge (from the PLL) plus a margin, modelled with set_clock_uncertainty always subtracted: it eats both setup and hold slack Shared clock path launch and capture clock paths share some buffers before they split, so their variations are correlated pessimism that was counted twice on the shared part is credited back (CPPR or CRPR)

Table 7.2 Clock non-idealities.

This is why CTS matters so much to timing: it is the tool's one chance to make latencies match and skew small. A well-balanced tree hands STA a clock that behaves almost ideally; a sloppy one hands it skew that becomes hold violations to be buffered away.

docs.title: Critical path, WNS and TNS
docs.text:
Slack is the single number that summarises a path. Two aggregate figures summarise a whole design.

  • The critical path is the path with the smallest (worst) slack; it sets the maximum clock frequency.
  • WNS, worst negative slack, is the most negative slack over all endpoints: how deep the hole is. WNS \(\ge 0\) means the whole design meets that check.
  • TNS, total negative slack, is the sum of the negative slacks over all failing endpoints (positive slacks count as zero): how wide the hole is, and how much work closure still needs.

A design with WNS \(= -0.4\) ns and TNS \(= -0.4\) ns has one lonely failing path. WNS \(= -0.4\) ns with TNS \(= -85\) ns has thousands of failing endpoints: something systemic, such as an over-ambitious clock or a bad corner, not a single fixable path.

Example 7.3: WNS and TNS from a list

Five endpoints have setup slacks \(+0.80\), \(-0.20\), \(-0.10\), \(+0.30\) and \(-0.40\) ns. The worst is \(-0.40\), so WNS \(= -0.40\) ns. Only the three negative values count in the total: TNS \(= -0.20 - 0.10 - 0.40 = -0.70\) ns. Three endpoints fail, the worst by 0.4 ns.

docs.title: A real timing report
docs.text:
This is roughly what OpenSTA or OpenROAD prints for report_checks -path_delay max.

Startpoint: ctrl_reg[3] (rising edge-triggered flip-flop clocked by clk)
Endpoint:   data_reg[7] (rising edge-triggered flip-flop clocked by clk)
Path Group: clk
Path Type:  max                          (a SETUP check)

  Delay    Time   Description
--------------------------------------------------------
   0.000   0.000  clock clk (rise edge)
   0.120   0.120  clock network delay (propagated)    <- launch latency
   0.000   0.120 ^ ctrl_reg[3]/CLK (sky130_fd_sc_hd__dfxtp_1)
   0.310   0.430 v ctrl_reg[3]/Q                      <- clock-to-Q
   0.240   0.670 ^ U231/X (sky130_fd_sc_hd__nand2_1)
   0.680   1.350 ^ U244/X (sky130_fd_sc_hd__and3_2)   <- the logic cone
   1.020   2.370 ^ U259/X (sky130_fd_sc_hd__buf_4)
   0.430   2.800 v data_reg[7]/D
           2.800  data arrival time

   5.000   5.000  clock clk (rise edge)              <- next capture edge, T = 5.0
   0.130   5.130  clock network delay (propagated)   <- capture latency
   0.000   5.130  clock reconvergence pessimism (CRPR)
  -0.300   4.830  library setup time
  -0.100   4.730  clock uncertainty
           4.730  data required time
--------------------------------------------------------
           4.730  data required time
          -2.800  data arrival time
--------------------------------------------------------
           1.930  slack (MET)

Read it from the top. The upper block builds the arrival time: the clock network delay to the launch flip-flop (0.120 ns), the clock-to-Q (0.310), then each gate and the final wire into the D pin. The lower block builds the required time: the next edge at 5.000 ns, plus the capture latency (0.130), minus the setup time (0.300) and the uncertainty (0.100). The last line, required minus arrival, is the slack. A hold report (-path_delay min) looks the same, but compares against the same edge and the slack must clear the hold time.

Example 7.4: Every number in the report

From the report above: launch latency 0.120 ns; clock-to-Q 0.310 ns; logic and wire delay \(0.240 + 0.680 + 1.020 + 0.430 = 2.370\) ns; arrival \(0.120 + 0.310 + 2.370 = 2.800\) ns; required 4.730 ns; slack \(+1.930\) ns. The single cell that contributes most delay is U259, a buf_4, at 1.020 ns; it is probably driving a long or heavily loaded net, and a fix would be to split its load, place it nearer its loads or re-buffer the net. Keeping everything else equal, the shortest period this path could meet follows from \(T + 0.130 - 0.300 - 0.100 \ge 2.800\), so \(T \ge 3.07\) ns, about 326 MHz.

docs.title: 7.6 Corners and variation
docs.text:
A cell's delay is not one number. It depends on Process (how the wafer came out), Voltage (supply droop) and Temperature. Libraries are measured at named PVT corners, one .lib per corner, and signoff must hold at all of them.

Corner Conditions Cells are Worst for SS (slow) slow silicon, low voltage, extreme temperature slowest, longest delays setup (latest arrival) TT (typical) nominal process, voltage and temperature nominal sanity checks and power FF (fast) fast silicon, high voltage fastest, shortest delays hold (data races through)

Table 7.3 The classic PVT corners.

The pairing is the crux. Setup is worst at the slow corner, where logic is sluggish and arrival is late; hold is worst at the fast corner, where logic is quick and data races. No single corner can therefore sign a design off: at the least, setup is closed at SS and hold at FF.

Temperature inversion

The intuition "hotter means slower" fails at low voltage in modern processes, Sky130 included. Below a crossover voltage, lower temperature makes cells slower, so the true worst setup corner may be the cold, low-voltage corner. This is why signoff enumerates corners exhaustively and does not trust a rule of thumb.

Multi-corner multi-mode (MCMM) analysis is the framework. A mode is a functional configuration with its own constraints and clocks (normal operation, scan test, low power). A corner is a PVT and wire-extraction condition (fast or slow wires too). The tool forms the cross-product, every mode at every relevant corner, and a path passes signoff only if it meets timing in all active scenarios. A real chip may have dozens.

On top of corners sits on-chip variation (OCV): even on one die, identical cells differ slightly. STA models this by derating, stretching the launch path's delays and shrinking the capture path's (for setup) to add pessimism. Advanced OCV (AOCV) makes the derate depend on path depth and distance, since long paths average out variation and need less margin; parametric methods (POCV) go further with statistical, sigma-based derates. CPPR then credits back the pessimism that was double counted on shared clock segments.

docs.title: 7.7 Fixing violations
docs.text:
When a report shows negative slack, the cure depends on which check failed, and the two are almost opposites.

Setup violation (path too slow) Hold violation (path too fast) Goal make the data arrive earlier make the data arrive later Fixes up-size slow cells, use faster (low-threshold) cells, restructure the logic cone, improve placement to cut wire delay, buffer long nets, add a pipeline stage, use useful skew; as a last resort slow the clock insert delay (buffer) cells on the fast path, down-size or swap to slower (high-threshold) cells, route the longer way; the clock period is irrelevant Goes back to synthesis (structure, cell choice), placement (wire length), CTS (useful skew) CTS (skew balance), routing (detours), placement (cell spacing)

Table 7.4 Setup and hold need opposite medicine.

The two fight. Hold buffers add area and can create new setup paths; the useful skew that helps setup can open a hold gap elsewhere. That is why timing closure is iterative, and why the slack left by earlier stages is so valuable. OpenROAD runs repair loops, repair_timing -setup and repair_timing -hold, that apply exactly these moves automatically; the intuition for what they are doing is what this chapter has built.

Common misconception

"If the design meets setup, it works." Setup is half the story. A design can pass every setup check with large positive slack and still be dead on arrival because one hold path fails at the fast corner, and unlike setup, you cannot slow the clock to rescue it. Meeting setup means it works at speed; meeting hold means it works at all. Both are mandatory for signoff.

Think about it

A register-to-register path has a comfortable \(+1.9\) ns of setup slack. You insert a big buffer to speed up a long net. Later a hold check on the same path fails. What did the buffer change?

Answer

The buffer changed the delay of the logic and wire on that path. If it sped up the fastest route through the logic, it reduced \(t_{logic,min}\). Hold depends on the fast case, \(t_{cq} + t_{logic,min}\), and not on the slow one, so a change that makes the fast route faster can push hold negative even while setup improves. Fixing one check can open a violation of the other.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• STA checks every path for setup and hold with no test vectors, using .lib, .spef and .sdc. The four path types are register to register, input to register, register to output and input to output.
  • Setup slack \(= (T + \text{skew} - t_{su} - t_{unc}) - (t_{cq} + t_{logic,max})\). Hold slack \(= (t_{cq} + t_{logic,min}) - (t_h + \text{skew} + t_{unc})\), independent of \(T\).
  • Skew helps one check and hurts the other; uncertainty hurts both. WNS is the depth of the worst failure and TNS its total width. A report builds arrival and required times line by line.
  • Setup is closed at the slow corner and hold at the fast corner, across all modes, with margins for on-chip variation; beware temperature inversion.
  • Fix setup by speeding paths up; fix hold by slowing them down.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 7.1: Slack by hand

A path has \(T = 5.0\), \(t_{cq} = 0.35\), slowest logic 4.10, fastest logic 0.20, \(t_{su} = 0.25\) and \(t_h = 0.10\) ns. (a) Find the setup slack, the hold slack and \(f_{max}\) with no skew. (b) Now let skew \(= +0.30\) and uncertainty \(= 0.10\). Find both slacks again. (c) At the slow corner every cell delay (clock-to-Q, logic, setup, hold) is multiplied by 1.25, and at the fast corner by 0.8; keep skew and uncertainty. Which check fails where?

Answer

(a) Setup \((5.0 - 0.25) - 4.45 = +0.30\) ns; hold \(0.55 - 0.10 = +0.45\) ns; \(f_{max} = 1/(0.35 + 4.10 + 0.25\ \text{ns}) = 1/4.70\ \text{ns} \approx 213\) MHz. (b) Setup \((5.0 + 0.30 - 0.25 - 0.10) - 4.45 = +0.50\) ns; hold \(0.55 - (0.10 + 0.30 + 0.10) = +0.05\) ns. (c) Slow corner: \(t_{cq} = 0.4375\), logic 5.125, \(t_{su} = 0.3125\), so setup \(= (5.0 + 0.30 - 0.3125 - 0.10) - (0.4375 + 5.125) = 4.8875 - 5.5625 = -0.675\) ns, which fails. Fast corner: \(t_{cq} = 0.28\), fastest logic 0.16, \(t_h = 0.08\), so hold \(= (0.28 + 0.16) - (0.08 + 0.30 + 0.10) = 0.44 - 0.48 = -0.04\) ns, which fails. Setup fails at the slow corner and hold at the fast corner, and both must be fixed: the classic corner pair.

Exercise 7.2: Setup and hold with skew and uncertainty

\(T = 2.0\) ns, \(t_{cq} = 0.15\), slowest logic 1.50, fastest logic 0.05, \(t_{su} = 0.10\), \(t_h = 0.20\), skew \(+0.10\), uncertainty \(0.05\) (ns). (a) Setup slack? (b) Hold slack? (c) Which fix would you apply?

Answer

(a) \((2.0 + 0.10 - 0.10 - 0.05) - (0.15 + 1.50) = 1.95 - 1.65 = +0.30\) ns, met. (b) \((0.15 + 0.05) - (0.20 + 0.10 + 0.05) = 0.20 - 0.35 = -0.15\) ns, violated. (c) Add about 0.15 ns of delay buffers on the short path. Setup has 0.30 ns to spare, so it can afford them; changing \(T\) would not help.

Exercise 7.3: Read a report

From the timing report in Section 7.5, state the launch latency, the clock-to-Q, the total logic delay, the arrival, the required time and the slack, and say which cell contributes the most delay.

Answer

Launch latency 0.120 ns; clock-to-Q 0.310 ns; logic and wire delay \(0.240 + 0.680 + 1.020 + 0.430 = 2.370\) ns; arrival 2.800 ns; required 4.730 ns; slack \(+1.930\) ns. The biggest single contributor is U259, a buf_4, at 1.020 ns. Without changing anything else the path could meet a period down to \(T \ge 3.07\) ns (about 326 MHz).

Exercise 7.4: Which fix?

Your run shows WNS \(= -0.2\) ns at the slow corner and a hold violation at the fast corner. Slowing the clock by 10 % makes the first go away. Why does it not fix the second, and what will?

Answer

Hold slack does not contain the clock period: launch and capture happen on the same edge. The cure is to make the short path slower, with delay buffers inserted after the clock tree (OpenROAD's repair_timing -hold), or to reduce the skew that hurts it.

Exercise 7.5: WNS and TNS

Two designs both have WNS \(= -0.4\) ns. Design A has TNS \(= -0.4\) ns and design B has TNS \(= -85\) ns. Which is nearer to closing, and why?

Answer

Design A. With TNS equal to WNS there is exactly one failing endpoint, a single path to fix. Design B has thousands of failing endpoints, which points to something systemic, such as an over-ambitious clock or the wrong corner.

Exercise 7.6: Set T very large

Set \(T\) to a huge value such as 1000 ns in the hold equation. Does the hold slack change? What does that say about running a chip slowly to be safe?

Answer

It does not change at all: \(T\) is absent from the hold equation. Running a chip more slowly can rescue a setup failure but never a hold failure, so "run slower to be safe" does not work for hold.

docs.title: Chapter 1: The RTL-to-GDSII Flow
docs.text:
This chapter draws the map of the whole territory before we study each region in turn. It names the eight stages that turn a hardware description into a manufacturable layout, says what goes into and comes out of each, and separates the front end, which decides what the logic is, from the back end, which decides where it goes. It then introduces the three things every later chapter takes for granted: the process design kit and its standard cells, the chain of files that carries the design from stage to stage, and the three goals (power, performance and area) between which every decision is a compromise. The chapter ends with the tools that do the work and with a warning about the commonest misunderstanding in the subject: that a design which simulates correctly is therefore a design that works.

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you can:

  1. Name the stages from RTL to GDSII and say what goes in and what comes out of each.
  2. Tell the front end from the back end.
  3. Explain what a PDK and a standard-cell library are, and why a chip is built from ready-made cells.
  4. Recognise the key file formats and state the power, performance and area trade-off.
  5. Name the open-source tools that do each job.

docs.title: 1.1 Two worlds
docs.text:
At one end of the flow is RTL, the register-transfer level: a description, in Verilog, SystemVerilog or VHDL, of a circuit as registers and the logic that computes each register's next value between clock edges. Two lines are enough to describe an adder whose result is captured on every clock edge:

always @(posedge clk)
  sum <= a + b;

At the other end is GDSII (Graphic Design System II), the industry-standard binary stream format for a finished layout. A GDSII file holds no logic at all. It is a database of polygons, millions of them, each on one of several dozen layers, and each layer corresponds to a mask that the factory will make. The whole subject of this book is the mechanical, and in the end provable, transformation of the first description into the second without changing what the circuit does.

The flow divides cleanly into two halves that even have different job titles.

The front end, or logic design, consists of writing the RTL, verifying it, and synthesising it into gates. Its product is a netlist: a list of ready-made gates and the wires that join them. The question the front end answers is what is the logic?

The back end, or physical design, takes the netlist and gives every gate and every wire a place and a shape on the silicon: floorplan, power, placement, clock tree, routing, extraction, signoff and GDSII. Its question is where does it go, and does it still work once the physics is included?

An analogy

Think of building a house. The front end is the architect's plan: which rooms there are and how they connect. The back end is the builders, who decide where every brick goes and where the pipes run, together with the inspector who checks that the walls stand up.

docs.title: 1.2 The eight stages
docs.text:
Figure 1.1 shows the eight stages in order, with the main file that each one hands to the next. Table 1.1 gives the question each stage answers.

Figure 1.1 The RTL-to-GDSII flow. The eight stages of the RTL-to-GDSII flow, from RTL and verification to the GDSII file, with the files handed on at each step. # Stage World In and out The question it answers 1 RTL design and verification Front end specification to .v plus testbench Does the logic do the right thing? 2 Logic synthesis Front end RTL, .sdc, .lib to gate netlist Which gates implement it, and are they fast enough? 3 Floorplanning and power Back end netlist, .lef to die, core and power grid How big is the chip, and how does power reach every gate? 4 Placement Back end floorplan to placed .def Where does every standard cell sit? 5 Clock-tree synthesis (CTS) Back end placed design to balanced clock network Does the clock reach every flip-flop at nearly the same moment? 6 Routing Back end placed design to routed .def Can every connection be drawn in metal, legally? 7 Extraction and timing signoff Back end routed design to .spef and timing reports With the real wires, is every path fast enough, and not too fast? 8 Physical verification and tapeout Back end layout to .gds, DRC and LVS clean Can the factory build it, and is it exactly the intended circuit?

Table 1.1 The stages of the flow.

Each of stages 2 to 8 has a chapter of its own, in this order. Verification of the RTL (stage 1) is the subject of the book on hardware description languages and is taken as given here.

docs.title: 1.3 What kind of chip?
docs.text:
"Turning RTL into hardware" means very different things depending on the target. The flow of this book targets a standard-cell ASIC, but it helps to know its neighbours.

Standard-cell ASIC FPGA Full custom What it is custom masks, built from a library of ready-made cells a reprogrammable fabric of lookup tables, multipliers and block RAM every transistor drawn by hand Design effort high: the full RTL-to-GDSII flow low to medium: synthesis and place-and-route in the vendor's tool extreme: months for a single block Up-front cost (NRE) very high; the course quotes $100k to $10M or more for a mask set almost none: you buy the chip the highest of all Cost per chip at volume lowest high, since you pay for unused fabric low, but rarely at scale Speed and power excellent modest; roughly 10 to 20 times the area of the equivalent ASIC and slower clocks the best possible Time to first chip months minutes, by recompiling a bitstream very long When to use it high volume, tight power and speed, cost-sensitive products prototypes, low volume, designs that must be updated in the field memories, analogue and radio blocks, clock generators, the very latest cells

Table 1.2 Three ways to turn a design into hardware. The cost figures are those quoted in the course material and are indicative only.

Rule of thumb

Prototype on an FPGA; build an ASIC once the volume pays for the masks; go full custom only for the few cells (memory bit cells, input and output circuits, clock generators) where a standard-cell library cannot compete. This book follows the ASIC path.

docs.title: 1.4 The PDK and the standard cells
docs.text:
A chip is never designed in the abstract. It is designed for one manufacturing process at one foundry, and everything needed to do that is packaged in the process design kit, or PDK: the geometric design rules, the transistor models, the definition of the mask layers and, most important for digital design, a standard-cell library.

A standard cell is a small, pre-designed and pre-measured logic gate: an inverter (INV), a two-input NAND (NAND2), a D flip-flop (DFF), a full adder, a buffer, often in several drive strengths (×1, ×2, ×4 and so on). The whole point of a standard-cell ASIC is that synthesis and place-and-route only ever arrange and connect these bricks and never touch an individual transistor.

All the cells of a library have the same height, a fixed number of routing tracks (the Sky130 high-density library uses a nine-track cell), and a width that depends on their complexity. Cells are placed side by side in horizontal rows. The power rail (VDD) runs along the top of every cell and the ground rail (VSS) along the bottom, so that when cells abut the rails join into continuous lines across the row. Because height never varies, a placer can pack thousands of cells like bricks.

Figure 1.2 A row of standard cells. A single row of standard cells of different widths and one common height, between a VDD rail above and a VSS rail below.

The tools never look inside a cell. Each cell comes with two abstract views:

Liberty (.lib) is the timing and power model. For every path from an input pin to an output pin it gives the delay and the output transition time as tables indexed by the input transition time and the output load; it gives setup and hold requirements for flip-flops; and it gives leakage and switching power. The numbers are obtained by circuit simulation at several operating conditions, called corners. Static timing analysis and synthesis read this file.

LEF (.lef), the Library Exchange Format, is the physical outline: the cell's bounding box, the positions of its pins, and the regions that are blocked. It is enough to place and wire the cell without revealing its inside. A companion technology LEF describes the metal layers, the vias and the routing rules.

Sky130, a real and free PDK

The SkyWater Sky130 kit is a 130 nm process and the first production-capable PDK released under a free licence. Its standard-cell families, such as sky130_fd_sc_hd (high density), ship the .lib, the .lef and the layout of every cell. That is exactly what makes the whole open-source flow, and this book's exercises, possible without signing a non-disclosure agreement.

docs.title: 1.5 A chain of files
docs.text:
The flow is really a chain of file transformations. Knowing what each format carries, and which stage produces and consumes it, is half the battle of learning the subject.

Extension Contents Made by, used by .v, .sv Verilog or SystemVerilog: the RTL, and later the gate-level netlist designer and synthesis, then simulation, synthesis, place-and-route, LVS .sdc Synopsys Design Constraints: clocks, input and output delays, false and multicycle paths designer, then synthesis, CTS, routing, timing .lib Liberty: characterised cell timing and power, one file per corner foundry, then synthesis and timing .lef cell outlines, metal layers, vias and rules PDK, then floorplan, placement, routing .def Design Exchange Format: component locations, nets and routes of the placed or routed design each layout stage, then the next stage, extraction, GDS writing .spef Standard Parasitic Exchange Format: the resistance and capacitance of every net extraction, then signoff timing and power analysis .gds, .oas GDSII, or its compact successor OASIS: the final polygons layout and tapeout, then mask making, DRC, LVS .sdf Standard Delay Format: per-instance delays timing, then gate-level timing simulation

Table 1.3 The main file formats of the flow.

docs.title: 1.6 Three goals: power, performance, area
docs.text:
Every decision in the flow is a negotiation among three quantities, abbreviated PPA.

Power is the sum of dynamic power (the energy of switching) and leakage. It is set by the supply voltage, by how often signals toggle, and by how many and what kind of cells are used. Lower is better for batteries and for heat.

Performance is the highest clock frequency the design can run at. It is limited by the slowest path between two registers. A faster clock needs larger, hungrier cells.

Area is silicon, and silicon is paid for by the square millimetre. A smaller die means more dice per wafer and so a cheaper chip, but leaves less room for the buffers that timing may need and makes wiring harder.

These pull against one another. Push frequency and you spend power and area on stronger cells and more buffers; shrink the area and congestion makes routing, and therefore timing, harder. Good design finds the balance that the specification asks for.

Timing closure is the name for making every timing path meet its target, under every operating condition, so that no path has negative slack. A single path that is 30 ps too slow means the chip fails at its target clock. Closure often dominates the back-end schedule: synthesis, sizing, placement, clock-tree synthesis and routing are tweaked, again and again, until the histogram of slacks is entirely non-negative.

docs.title: 1.7 Open-source and commercial tools
docs.text:
The same flow can be run with the large commercial suites or with free tools. This book teaches the open-source stack because you can run every step yourself, today, at no cost.

Job Open source Commercial Synthesis Yosys Design Compiler, Genus Floorplan, placement, CTS, routing, timing OpenROAD IC Compiler II, Innovus; PrimeTime, Tempus Layout, rule checks, GDS Magic, KLayout Calibre, IC Validator, Pegasus Layout-versus-netlist check netgen Calibre LVS, Pegasus The whole flow in one command OpenLANE in-house scripts and vendor reference flows

Table 1.4 Open-source and commercial tools for each job.

With OpenLANE the whole flow, from RTL and a configuration file to a GDSII layout, is a single command; Chapter 9 explains it in detail.

# The whole flow, one command, in OpenLANE
./flow.tcl -design spm            # RTL (.v) + config -> GDSII

# Under the hood it runs, roughly:
#   yosys     synthesis                              -> netlist.v
#   openroad  floorplan, place, cts, route           -> final.def
#   magic     DEF -> GDS, DRC
#   netgen    LVS (layout versus schematic)

docs.title: 1.8 "It simulates, so it works": not quite
docs.text:
Common misconception

"Once my Verilog simulates correctly, the chip works." Functional simulation checks the logic and ignores the physics. Real wires have resistance and capacitance. Gates take time, more when hot and less when the supply voltage is high. The clock reaches different flip-flops at slightly different moments. A logically perfect design can still fail on silicon because a signal arrives too late (a setup violation) or, surprisingly, too early (a hold violation).

That is why the back end exists: to place and wire the design and then to re-check it with real delays. Extraction and static timing signoff, Chapters 6 and 7, are the stages that bring the physics back.

Think about it

Synthesis needs the .lib to know cell delays, but accurate delays also depend on wire parasitics that do not exist until after placement and routing. How does synthesis estimate timing before any wires exist?

Answer

It uses wire-load models, statistical guesses of the capacitance of a net from its fan-out, or in modern flows a rough placement. The estimate is refined at every later stage as real locations and real wires become known. This chicken-and-egg loop is why the flow iterates and why slack left over by an early stage is so valuable later.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• RTL-to-GDSII turns a behavioural description into manufacturable polygons without changing what the circuit does.
  • The front end is RTL, verification and synthesis, ending in a netlist. The back end is floorplan, power, placement, clock tree, routing, extraction and timing, physical verification and GDSII.
  • A standard-cell ASIC is built only from the ready-made cells of one foundry's PDK; each cell has a .lib timing view and a .lef physical view.
  • The design passes through a chain of files: .v and .sdc, then .def and .spef, and finally .gds.
  • Power, performance and area pull against each other; timing closure, making every path meet timing at every corner, is usually the hardest part.
  • Yosys, OpenROAD, Magic, KLayout and netgen, orchestrated by OpenLANE, form a complete free flow.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1.1: The flow in order

Put these stages in flow order: routing, synthesis, clock tree, floorplan, extraction and timing, placement, physical verification.

Answer

Synthesis, floorplan, placement, clock tree, routing, extraction and timing, physical verification.

Exercise 1.2: Files

For each of .sdc, .lib, .lef, .def, .spef and .gds, say which stage produces it and which stages use it.

Answer
  • .sdc: written by the designer; read by synthesis, the layout stages and timing analysis.
  • .lib and .lef: supplied by the PDK; .lib is read by synthesis and timing, .lef by the layout tools.
  • .def: produced by each layout stage (floorplan, placement, CTS, routing) and read by the next one.
  • .spef: produced by extraction and read by signoff timing.
  • .gds: written at the end of layout and sent to the foundry; also read by DRC and LVS.

Exercise 1.3: Where do you go back to?

Which stage would you revisit for (a) a hold violation found after routing, (b) a die that is too big, (c) a functional bug found in gate-level simulation?

Answer

(a) The clock tree or routing, where hold buffers and skew are handled. (b) The floorplan: utilisation and aspect ratio. (c) The RTL itself. Synthesis only preserves the logic it is given, bugs included.

Exercise 1.4: Why the PDK first?

Why does an ASIC design need the foundry's PDK before synthesis can even start?

Answer

Synthesis builds the design only from the foundry's standard cells, and it needs their timing (.lib) to choose among them. With no library there are no gates to map to.

Exercise 1.5: Choosing a target

A start-up needs 500 units of a signal-processing board for field trials, and the algorithm is likely to change twice before launch. Which of the three targets in Table 1.2 would you choose, and why?

Answer

An FPGA. The volume is far too small to repay an ASIC mask set, the design must be updated in the field, and the time to a working board is minutes rather than months. An ASIC becomes attractive only if the product succeeds and the volume grows, and full custom is not justified at all.
